query.original_query: single-cell foundation model developmental trajectory pseudotime directionality RNA velocity irreversibility representation

sub_queries.semantic_query: internal representation of developmental trajectory pseudotime directionality and RNA velocity irreversibility in single-cell foundation models, probing cell state and temporal ordering in latent space
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigate how single-cell foundation models encode developmental trajectory pseudotime directionality and RNA velocity irreversibility within their latent representations. Using linear probing and activation patching on the latent space of scGPT and Geneformer, we analyze whether cell state ordering along a continuous developmental axis is linearly decodable from the model’s embeddings. Our analysis reveals that pseudotime directionality is represented in a low-dimensional subspace, with the first principal component of the latent space strongly correlating with temporal ordering. However, we find that RNA velocity irreversibility—the asymmetry between forward and backward transitions—is not consistently encoded across cell types. Causal mediation analysis on attention heads shows that specific layers contribute disproportionately to directional signals, while others encode static cell-type identity. Results indicate that these models capture a smoothed, monotonic trajectory but lack explicit representation of irreversible dynamics, suggesting a reliance on static state features rather than true temporal directionality.

sub_queries.semantic_query: single-cell RNA sequencing developmental trajectory inference pseudotime ordering RNA velocity directionality irreversibility cell fate decision dynamical systems modeling
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigate the relationship between pseudotime ordering inferred from single-cell RNA sequencing data and the directionality of cellular transitions predicted by RNA velocity analysis. Using dynamical systems modeling, we test the hypothesis that developmental trajectories, as reconstructed by diffusion-based pseudotime algorithms, exhibit measurable irreversibility consistent with a non-equilibrium attractor landscape. We applied both a minimum spanning tree-based pseudotime method and a steady-state RNA velocity model to a publicly available dataset of differentiating hematopoietic stem cells. Results indicate a significant concordance between the pseudotime axis and the vector field of spliced-to-unspliced mRNA ratios, particularly along the erythroid and myeloid branches. However, we observed local regions of velocity-pseudotime discordance, suggesting transient cell fate decisions or technical noise in velocity estimation. Findings support the hypothesis that RNA velocity directionality can validate pseudotime ordering, but also highlight that the assumption of a continuous, monotonic trajectory may obscure branching dynamics. These results underscore the utility of combining pseudotime inference with velocity-based dynamical systems for resolving cell fate commitment.

papers.title: Learning Causal Representations of Single Cells via Sparse Mechanism Shift Modeling
papers.research_question: How can we learn causal representations of single-cell genomics data by modeling perturbations as interventions on latent variables, leveraging the sparse mechanism shift assumption to improve disentanglement, causal target identification, and out-of-domain generalization?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes sVAE+, a Bayesian variant of the sparse VAE for single-cell perturbation data, which models perturbations as stochastic interventions on a sparse subset of latent variables, and demonstrates that it outperforms existing methods in disentanglement, causal target identification, and out-of-domain generalization.
papers.conclusion: Modeling perturbations as interventions with sparse mechanism shift enables learning causal representations that are more interpretable and generalize better, offering a promising approach for single-cell genomics and perturbation biology.
papers.key_findings:
sVAE+ achieves higher disentanglement scores (MCC) compared to VAE, β-VAE, iVAE, and sVAE on simulated data.
sVAE+ better recovers the causal graph (higher precision, recall, F1) of intervention targets in latent space.
sVAE+ improves out-of-domain generalization, yielding lower interventional negative log-likelihood on held-out perturbations.
On real single-cell perturbation datasets, sVAE+ outperforms other methods in transfer learning tasks.
The sparse mechanism shift assumption is beneficial for learning interpretable causal representations from single-cell perturbation data.
papers.limitation:
The sparsity assumption may be limiting due to indirect downstream effects in biological systems, especially as time passes after the initial perturbation.
The model assumes discrete interventions and may not handle time-resolved measurements without extension.
future_direction: Incorporating time-resolved measurements from single-cell perturbation experiments.
Handling non-sparse interactions and feedback mechanisms in biological pathways.
Extending the noise model to more realistic distributions for scRNA-seq data.
papers.abstract: Latent variable models such as the Variational Auto-Encoder (VAE) have become a go-to tool for analyzing biological data, especially in the field of single-cell genomics. One remaining challenge is the interpretability of latent variables as biological processes that define a cell's identity. Outside of biological applications, this problem is commonly referred to as learning disentangled representations. Although several disentanglement-promoting variants of the VAE were introduced, and applied to single-cell genomics data, this task has been shown to be infeasible from independent and identically distributed measurements, without additional structure. Instead, recent methods propose to leverage non-stationary data, as well as the sparse mechanism shift assumption in order to learn disentangled representations with a causal semantic. Here, we extend the application of these methodological advances to the analysis of single-cell genomics data with genetic or chemical perturbations. More precisely, we propose a deep generative model of single-cell gene expression data for which each perturbation is treated as a stochastic intervention targeting an unknown, but sparse, subset of latent variables. We benchmark these methods on simulated single-cell data to evaluate their performance at latent units recovery, causal target identification and out-of-domain generalization. Finally, we apply those approaches to two real-world large-scale gene perturbation data sets and find that models that exploit the sparse mechanism shift hypothesis surpass contemporary methods on a transfer learning task. We implement our new model and benchmarks using the scvi-tools library, and release it as open-source software at https://github.com/Genentech/sVAE.

papers.title: Systematic Evaluation of Single-Cell Foundation Model Interpretability Reveals Attention Captures Co-Expression Rather Than Unique Regulatory Signal
papers.research_question: Does attention in single-cell foundation models capture causal regulatory relationships or just co-expression? Do attention-derived edge scores provide incremental value beyond gene-level features for predicting perturbation outcomes?
papers.core_contribution: Attention patterns in single-cell foundation models encode structured biological information (e.g., protein-protein interactions in early layers, transcriptional regulation in late layers) but do not capture causal regulatory signal; they provide no incremental value over gene-level features for predicting perturbation outcomes.
papers.conclusion: Attention patterns in single-cell foundation models capture co-expression rather than causal regulatory signal, and the proposed evaluation framework provides a reusable quality-control standard for mechanistic interpretability in this domain.
papers.key_findings:
Attention patterns show layer-specific biological specialization but do not outperform trivial gene-level baselines for perturbation prediction.
Pairwise edge scores (attention or correlation) provide no incremental predictive value beyond gene-level features.
Causal ablation of 'regulatory' attention heads does not degrade perturbation prediction, indicating distributed redundancy.
The relationship between attention and correlation is context-dependent across cell types and perturbation modalities.
Cell-State Stratified Interpretability (CSSI) improves attention-derived GRN recovery by controlling for heterogeneity.
papers.limitation:
Causal ablation only performed on Geneformer V2-316M, not on scGPT due to architectural differences.
Perturbation data limited to four cell types and two modalities; additional tissues, species, and architectures remain untested.
No decisive positive control demonstrates recovery of known causal regulatory structure in a realistic perturbation setting.
future_direction: Test additional tissues, species, and architectures (e.g., scFoundation).
Focus interpretability efforts on residual-stream geometry, MLP-stored knowledge, or representations from the full forward pass.
papers.abstract: We present a systematic evaluation framework - thirty-seven analyses, 153 statistical tests, four cell types, two perturbation modalities - for assessing mechanistic interpretability in single-cell foundation models. Applying this framework to scGPT and Geneformer, we find that attention patterns encode structured biological information with layer-specific organisation - protein-protein interactions in early layers, transcriptional regulation in late layers - but this structure provides no incremental value for perturbation prediction: trivial gene-level baselines outperform both attention and correlation edges (AUROC 0.81-0.88 versus 0.70), pairwise edge scores add zero predictive contribution, and causal ablation of regulatory heads produces no degradation. These findings generalise from K562 to RPE1 cells; the attention-correlation relationship is context-dependent, but gene-level dominance is universal. Cell-State Stratified Interpretability (CSSI) addresses an attention-specific scaling failure, improving GRN recovery up to 1.85x. The framework establishes reusable quality-control standards for the field.

papers.title: pmVAE: Learning Interpretable Single-Cell Representations with Pathway Modules
papers.research_question: How to learn interpretable single-cell representations by incorporating pathway information into a VAE architecture, addressing pathway correlation and hierarchical structure?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces pmVAE, a variational autoencoder that learns interpretable single-cell representations by factorizing the latent space according to pathway gene sets, and addresses pathway correlation through a module-specific training procedure.
papers.conclusion: pmVAE is an effective method for learning interpretable multidimensional pathway representations from single-cell data, revealing pathway-specific responses and effects.
papers.key_findings:
pmVAE outperforms baseline methods (f-scLVM and interpretable AE) in discriminative accuracy for pathway activity.
Multidimensional pathway representations are necessary to explain context-dependent pathway effects.
pmVAE's pathway modules capture biologically relevant signals, such as cell-type specific responses to interferon stimulation.
papers.limitation: The independence enforced between pathway modules ignores known pathway-pathway interactions arising from signaling effects.
future_direction: Incorporating known signaling interactions into the architecture to model pathway-pathway interactions.
Extending pmVAE to integrate multiple omics technologies.
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Motivation Deep learning techniques have yielded tremendous progress in the field of computational biology over the last decade, however many of these techniques are opaque to the user. To provide interpretable results, methods have incorporated biological priors directly into the learning task; one such biological prior is pathway structure. While pathways represent most biological processes in the cell, the high level of correlation and hierarchical structure make it complicated to determine an appropriate computational representation. Results Here, we present pathway module Variational Autoencoder (pmVAE). Our method encodes pathway information by restricting the structure of our VAE to mirror gene-pathway memberships. Its architecture is composed of a set of subnetworks, which we refer to as pathway modules. The subnetworks learn interpretable latent representations by factorizing the latent space according to pathway gene sets. We directly address correlation between pathways by balancing a module-specific local loss and a global reconstruction loss. Furthermore, since many pathways are by nature hierarchical and therefore the product of multiple downstream signals, we model each pathway as a multidimensional vector. Due to their factorization over pathways, the representations allow for easy and interpretable analysis of multiple downstream effects, such as cell type and biological stimulus, within the contexts of each pathway. We compare pmVAE against two other state-of-the-art methods on two single-cell RNA-seq case-control data sets, demonstrating that our pathway representations are both more discriminative and consistent in detecting pathways targeted by a perturbation. Availability and implementation https://github.com/ratschlab/pmvae

papers.title: Transcoder-based Circuit Analysis for Interpretable Single-Cell Foundation Models
papers.research_question: How can transcoders be used to extract interpretable decision-making circuits from single-cell foundation models, and do these circuits correspond to biological mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that applying transcoders to single-cell foundation models enables the extraction of biologically interpretable internal decision circuits, confirming the potential of this approach for mechanistic interpretability in computational biology.
papers.conclusion: Transcoders provide a viable method for extracting interpretable circuits from single-cell foundation models, opening new avenues for interpretability research in this domain, though manual interpretation remains a limitation.
papers.key_findings:
Transcoders can be successfully trained on the C2S model, capturing significant MLP functionality as shown by validation loss comparison.
Human evaluation of transcoder features revealed that 35% of randomly selected features were gene-level interpretable.
Extracted circuits for cell type classification include features corresponding to biologically relevant genes such as VWF, PTPRB, and SPARCL1.
The transcoder-replaced model has lower validation loss than a model with MLPs removed, indicating effective approximation.
Circuit tracing identifies computational paths involving attention and MLP features that contribute to predictions.
papers.limitation:
Biological interpretation of extracted circuits was performed manually, which is time-consuming and potentially subjective.
The choice of training dataset significantly impacts the features learned by transcoders, limiting generalizability.
future_direction: Develop automated interpretation methods to systematically map transcoder features to biological concepts.
Explore other datasets to reveal more general features and circuits across different biological contexts.
Develop novel methods to further enhance scFM interpretability and apply these techniques to discover new biological insights.
papers.abstract: Single-cell foundation models (scFMs) have demonstrated state-of-the-art performance on various tasks, such as cell-type annotation and perturbation response prediction, by learning gene regulatory networks from large-scale transcriptome data. However, a significant challenge remains: the decision-making processes of these models are less interpretable compared to traditional methods like differential gene expression analysis. Recently, transcoders have emerged as a promising approach for extracting interpretable decision circuits from large language models (LLMs). In this work, we train a transcoder on the cell2sentence (C2S) model, a state-of-the-art scFM. By leveraging the trained transcoder, we extract internal decision-making circuits from the C2S model. We demonstrate that the discovered circuits correspond to real-world biological mechanisms, confirming the potential of transcoders to uncover biologically plausible pathways within complex single-cell models.

papers.title: Slowness and Sparseness Lead to Place, Head-Direction, and Spatial-View Cells
papers.research_question: How can place cells, head-direction cells, and spatial-view cells self-organize from unsupervised learning on visual stimuli, and how does the movement pattern of the animal affect the type of cells that develop?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that place cells, head-direction cells, and spatial-view cells can emerge from an unsupervised learning model based on slowness (Slow Feature Analysis) and sparseness principles applied to visual input, with the cell type depending solely on the movement statistics of the simulated animal.
papers.conclusion: A purely sensory-driven unsupervised system can reproduce key properties of oriospatial cells (place, head-direction, spatial-view, and to some extent grid cells), with the output characteristics depending solely on the movement statistics.
papers.key_findings:
The same hierarchical SFA model can develop place cells, head-direction cells, or spatial-view cells depending on the movement pattern (relative rotational speed) of the simulated animal.
The SFA layer extracts a distributed, grid-like representation of position and orientation, which is then transformed into localized fields via sparse coding (ICA or competitive learning).
A mathematical analysis accurately predicts the output of the top SFA layer, showing that the slowest features correspond to Fourier-like basis functions in the configuration space.
Learning rate adaptation (LRA) based on vestibular-like signals allows concurrent learning of place cells and head-direction cells from the same movement statistics.
The model is purely sensory-driven and memoryless, demonstrating that complex spatial representations can form without path integration or explicit memory.
papers.limitation:
The model is memoryless and purely sensory-driven, so it cannot perform path integration.
The environment is static during training, which is not realistic.
The implementation of SFA (eigenvalue problem) and ICA (CuBICA) might not be biologically plausible.
future_direction: Extend the model to dynamic environments with changing variables (e.g., lighting).
Integrate other modalities such as olfactory cues.
Test the model's predictions experimentally, e.g., by manipulating movement statistics to influence cell invariance properties.
papers.abstract: We present a model for the self-organized formation of place cells, head-direction cells, and spatial-view cells in the hippocampal formation based on unsupervised learning on quasi-natural visual stimuli. The model comprises a hierarchy of Slow Feature Analysis (SFA) nodes, which were recently shown to reproduce many properties of complex cells in the early visual system []. The system extracts a distributed grid-like representation of position and orientation, which is transcoded into a localized place-field, head-direction, or view representation, by sparse coding. The type of cells that develops depends solely on the relevant input statistics, i.e., the movement pattern of the simulated animal. The numerical simulations are complemented by a mathematical analysis that allows us to accurately predict the output of the top SFA layer.

papers.title: SAE-RNA: A Sparse Autoencoder Model for Interpreting RNA Language Model Representations
papers.research_question: How and what do RNA Language Models internally encode about messenger RNA (mRNA) or non-coding RNA (ncRNA) families?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SAE-RNA, a sparse autoencoder model that interprets RNA language model representations by discovering sparse features aligned with biological structures and ncRNA families.
papers.conclusion: SAE-RNA provides a method for concept discovery in pretrained RNA LM embeddings, enabling interpretation without retraining and offering features for downstream tasks like feature-aware fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
SAE features localize in structurally meaningful regions such as stems and hairpins.
Features exhibit sequence biases like poly-G/C/A/U tracts that map onto secondary-structure contexts.
Deeper layers transition from diffuse to type-selective activations, with a small subset of channels preferentially firing for specific ncRNA families.
The last layer shows diminished signal, suggesting late-stage representational compression.
Features can be annotated using LLM prompting to align with known biological motifs.
papers.limitation:
Computational constraints restricted the scale of training data used for the SAE models.
SAE training outcomes can vary depending on hyperparameter choices, such as sparsity setting, which may influence the granularity and stability of learned features.
future_direction: Feature-aware fine-tuning with SAE-derived features for downstream RNA tasks.
papers.abstract: Deep learning, particularly with the advancement of Large Language Models, has transformed biomolecular modeling, with protein advances (e.g., ESM) inspiring emerging RNA language models such as RiNALMo. Yet how and what these RNA Language Models internally encode about messenger RNA (mRNA) or non-coding RNA (ncRNA) families remains unclear. We present SAE- RNA, interpretability model that analyzes RiNALMo representations and maps them to known human-level biological features. Our work frames RNA interpretability as concept discovery in pretrained embeddings, without end-to-end retraining, and provides practical tools to probe what RNA LMs may encode about ncRNA families. The model can be extended to close comparisons between RNA groups, and supporting hypothesis generation about previously unrecognized relationships.

papers.title: Discovering Interpretable Biological Concepts in Single-cell RNA-seq Foundation Models
papers.research_question: How can we extract and interpret biological concepts from single-cell RNA-seq foundation models to improve their interpretability and utility for biological discovery?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a novel concept-based interpretability framework for single-cell RNA-seq models, featuring an attribution method with counterfactual perturbations and two complementary interpretation approaches (expert-driven and ontology-driven), demonstrating that extracted concepts are more interpretable than individual neurons.
papers.conclusion: This work provides a principled framework for interpreting what biological knowledge foundation models have encoded, paving the way for their use for hypothesis generation and discovery.
papers.key_findings:
Concepts extracted by Sparse Auto-Encoders (SAEs) are more interpretable than individual neurons from the model's latent space.
The proposed attribution method with counterfactual perturbations identifies genes that influence concept activation, moving beyond correlational approaches.
Some concepts are stable across different datasets, indicating reliable extraction of biological signals.
Concept activations preserve predictive performance for downstream tasks like cell type and cell cycle phase classification.
The framework enables interpretation of concepts as specific cell types, tissues, or biological processes.
papers.limitation:
Nearly half of the extracted concepts could not be interpreted by either the domain expert or the pathway enrichment method, potentially due to limitations in current biological knowledge or the interpretation tools.
SAEs show a drop in reconstruction performance (R2) when applied to an unseen dataset, especially for scGPT due to differences in input gene sets between datasets.
Pathway enrichment interpretation is limited by the incompleteness of gene annotations and the ontology structure, potentially biasing interpretation towards known knowledge.
future_direction: Integrate additional knowledge sources (e.g., The Protein Atlas, PubMed articles) into the visualization platform to further assist experts in concept interpretation.
Investigate the behavior of gene perturbations on model embeddings, as their impact differs between scGPT and scVI.
papers.abstract: Single-cell RNA-seq foundation models achieve strong performance on downstream tasks but remain black boxes, limiting their utility for biological discovery. Recent work has shown that sparse dictionary learning can extract concepts from deep learning models, with promising applications in biomedical imaging and protein models. However, interpreting biological concepts remains challenging, as biological sequences are not inherently human-interpretable. We introduce a novel concept-based interpretability framework for single-cell RNA-seq models with a focus on concept interpretation and evaluation. We propose an attribution method with counterfactual perturbations that identifies genes that influence concept activation, moving beyond correlational approaches like differential expression analysis. We then provide two complementary interpretation approaches: an expert-driven analysis facilitated by an interactive interface and an ontology-driven method with attribution-based biological pathway enrichment. Applying our framework to two well-known single-cell RNA-seq models from the literature, we interpret concepts extracted by Top-K Sparse Auto-Encoders trained on two immune cell datasets. With a domain expert in immunology, we show that concepts improve interpretability compared to individual neurons while preserving the richness and informativeness of the latent representations. This work provides a principled framework for interpreting what biological knowledge foundation models have encoded, paving the way for their use for hypothesis generation and discovery.

papers.title: Representation learning of genomic sequence motifs with convolutional neural networks
papers.research_question: How does CNN architecture, specifically convolutional filter size and max-pooling, influence the extent that sequence motif representations are learned by first layer filters?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that CNN architecture controls whether first layer filters learn whole motif representations (localist) or partial motifs (distributed), with large max-pooling limiting hierarchical learning and encouraging interpretable filters.
papers.conclusion: Architectural design of CNNs can be used to intentionally learn interpretable representations in first layer filters, with a trade-off in performance, providing guidance for model interpretability in genomics.
papers.key_findings:
Large max-pool sizes relative to filter size encourage first layer filters to learn whole motif representations.
Small max-pool sizes allow deeper layers to assemble partial motifs into whole motifs, leading to distributed representations in first layer.
The representation learning principles generalize from synthetic sequences to in vivo genomic data.
Overparameterizing the number of first layer filters reduces the fraction that learn motifs due to optimization dynamics.
Filter size alone is not sufficient; the ability to assemble motifs in deeper layers is key.
papers.limitation:
Filter visualization does not specify the importance of filters or how they are combined for predictions.
The study uses a simplifying assumption that TF binding sites are represented by single PWM-like motifs, which may not hold in vivo.
future_direction: Quantifying the importance of filters that learn motifs.
Exploring how these principles apply to more complex regulatory codes.
papers.abstract: Although convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have been applied to a variety of computational genomics problems, there remains a large gap in our understanding of how they build representations of regulatory genomic sequences. Here we perform systematic experiments on synthetic sequences to reveal how CNN architecture, specifically convolutional filter size and max-pooling, influences the extent that sequence motif representations are learned by first layer filters. We find that CNNs designed to foster hierarchical representation learning of sequence motifs-assembling partial features into whole features in deeper layers-tend to learn distributed representations, i.e. partial motifs. On the other hand, CNNs that are designed to limit the ability to hierarchically build sequence motif representations in deeper layers tend to learn more interpretable localist representations, i.e. whole motifs. We then validate that this representation learning principle established from synthetic sequences generalizes to in vivo sequences.

papers.title: Time-Evolving Dynamical System for Learning Latent Representations of Mouse Visual Neural Activity
papers.research_question: How to extract high-quality latent representations from visual neural activity that capture temporal dynamics and disentangle stimulus-relevant components from internal states?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes TE-ViDS, a sequential latent variable model that evolves two parts of latent representations over time to disentangle stimulus-relevant components from internal states in visual neural activity, achieving state-of-the-art decoding performance and providing insights into visual processing.
papers.conclusion: TE-ViDS is markedly competent in extracting stimulus-relevant embeddings from visual neural activity and contributes to the understanding of visual processing mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
TE-ViDS achieves the best decoding performance on natural scenes and natural movies compared to alternative models.
TE-ViDS extracts interpretable latent trajectories that uncover clear underlying neural dynamics.
TE-ViDS provides new insights into differences in visual information processing between subjects and between cortical regions.
The external latent representations are tuned to stimulus-relevant components, while internal latent representations reflect internal states.
The model's performance varies across mouse visual cortical regions, with primary and mid-level regions showing higher decoding performance than high-level regions.
papers.limitation:
In the absence of recorded internal states or behavioral information, it is difficult to quantitatively assess the interpretability of internal latent variables and interpret their functional role.
The model exhibits substantial variability in decoding performance across individual mice, which may be due to variability in neural activity between subjects and trials.
future_direction: Extend the approach to neural data from other species and modalities to investigate broader principles of biological coding mechanisms.
Further exploration is required to consistently construct high-quality stimulus-correlated latent representations across conditions.
papers.abstract: Seeking high-quality representations with latent variable models (LVMs) to reveal the intrinsic correlation between neural activity and behavior or sensory stimuli has attracted much interest. In the study of the biological visual system, naturalistic visual stimuli are inherently high-dimensional and time-dependent, leading to intricate dynamics within visual neural activity. However, most work on LVMs has not explicitly considered neural temporal relationships. To cope with such conditions, we propose Time-Evolving Visual Dynamical System (TE-ViDS), a sequential LVM that decomposes neural activity into low-dimensional latent representations that evolve over time. To better align the model with the characteristics of visual neural activity, we split latent representations into two parts and apply contrastive learning to shape them. Extensive experiments on synthetic datasets and real neural datasets from the mouse visual cortex demonstrate that TE-ViDS achieves the best decoding performance on naturalistic scenes/movies, extracts interpretable latent trajectories that uncover clear underlying neural dynamics, and provides new insights into differences in visual information processing between subjects and between cortical regions. In summary, TE-ViDS is markedly competent in extracting stimulus-relevant embeddings from visual neural activity and contributes to the understanding of visual processing mechanisms. Our codes are available at https://github.com/Grasshlw/Time-Evolving-Visual-Dynamical-System.

papers.title: Manifolds and Modules: How Function Develops in a Neural Foundation Model
papers.research_question: Do neural decoding and encoding manifolds reveal new insights into how foundation models represent temporal response patterns? Are the representations brain-like?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes a neural foundation model (FNN) using decoding/encoding manifolds and trajectories, finding that different processing stages (encoder, recurrent, readout) exhibit distinct representational structures. The recurrent module enriches temporal representations, while the readout achieves biological fidelity through numerous specialized feature maps rather than biologically plausible mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: Neural foundation models may be more similar in internal operation to other foundation models than to their biological counterparts. Future architectures incorporating recurrence after a light-weight retinal-like encoder and constraining feature dimensionality to match biological cell type diversity could bridge the gap between computational performance and biological plausibility.
papers.key_findings:
The feedforward encoder module lacks biologically plausible stimulus-dependent temporal patterns and mainly reports input features with varying intensity.
The recurrent module shows a jump in capabilities by 'pushing apart' representations of different temporal stimulus patterns, enabling better stimulus separability.
The readout module accounts for biological variability by relying on a large number of self-similar feature maps, differing from known biological counterparts in V1.
The output layer achieves a continuous representation by linearly combining the readout features to associate spike trains with input movies.
The model's internal dynamics (quantified by tubularity metrics) are less complex and entangled than those observed in biological retina and V1 data.
papers.limitation:
The analysis utilized a single foundation model, due to the limited availability of other video-based foundation models of neural activity over time.
The work used a restricted set of stimuli to ensure comparability to biological results.
future_direction: Future architectures incorporating recurrence directly after a more light-weight retinal-like encoder.
Constraining feature dimensionality to match biological cell type diversity to yield models that bridge the gap between computational performance and biological plausibility.
papers.abstract: Foundation models have shown remarkable success in fitting biological visual systems; however, their black-box nature inherently limits their utility for understanding brain function. Here, we peek inside a SOTA foundation model of neural activity (Wang et al., 2025) as a physiologist might, characterizing each 'neuron' based on its temporal response properties to parametric stimuli. We analyze how different stimuli are represented in neural activity space by building decoding manifolds, and we analyze how different neurons are represented in stimulus-response space by building neural encoding manifolds. We find that the different processing stages of the model (i.e., the feedforward encoder, recurrent, and readout modules) each exhibit qualitatively different representational structures in these manifolds. The recurrent module shows a jump in capabilities over the encoder module by 'pushing apart' the representations of different temporal stimulus patterns; while the readout module achieves biological fidelity by using numerous specialized feature maps rather than biologically plausible mechanisms. Overall, we present this work as a study of the inner workings of a prominent neural foundation model, gaining insights into the biological relevance of its internals through the novel analysis of its neurons' joint temporal response patterns.

papers.title: Interpretable statistical representations of neural population dynamics and geometry
papers.research_question: How can we learn interpretable and consistent latent representations of neural population dynamics that evolve on low-dimensional manifolds, and how can we compare these dynamics across conditions, networks, and animals?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MARBLE, an unsupervised geometric deep learning method that learns interpretable latent representations of neural population dynamics by decomposing them into local flow fields, enabling consistent comparison of dynamics across networks and animals.
papers.conclusion: Our results suggest that manifold structure provides a powerful inductive bias to develop powerful decoding algorithms and assimilate data across experiments.
papers.key_findings:
MARBLE discovers low-dimensional latent representations that parametrize high-dimensional neural dynamics during gain modulation, decision-making, and changes in internal state.
MARBLE representations are consistent across neural networks and animals, enabling robust comparison of cognitive computations.
MARBLE outperforms current representation learning approaches (CEBRA, LFADS) in within- and across-animal decoding accuracy.
MARBLE can detect dynamical events such as bifurcations in RNNs corresponding to loss of task performance.
MARBLE can reveal the global geometric structure of latent states (e.g., circular arrangement for reaching directions) without behavioral supervision.
papers.abstract: The dynamics of neuron populations commonly evolve on low-dimensional manifolds. Thus, we need methods that learn the dynamical processes over neural manifolds to infer interpretable and consistent latent representations. We introduce a representation learning method, MARBLE, that decomposes on-manifold dynamics into local flow fields and maps them into a common latent space using unsupervised geometric deep learning. In simulated non-linear dynamical systems, recurrent neural networks, and experimental single-neuron recordings from primates and rodents, we discover emergent low-dimensional latent representations that parametrise high-dimensional neural dynamics during gain modulation, decision-making, and changes in the internal state. These representations are consistent across neural networks and animals, enabling the robust comparison of cognitive computations. Extensive benchmarking demonstrates state-of-the-art within- and across-animal decoding accuracy of MARBLE compared with current representation learning approaches, with minimal user input. Our results suggest that manifold structure provides a powerful inductive bias to develop powerful decoding algorithms and assimilate data across experiments.

papers.title: Virtual perturbations to assess explainability of deep-learning based cell fate predictors
papers.research_question: How can virtual perturbations be used to assess the explainability of deep learning models and discover causal relationships between input features and model outputs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces virtual perturbation, a technique for assessing the impact of input features on model outputs by making systematic alterations to input data or internal representations, and applies it to a cell fate prediction model to confirm the model learned the importance of nuclear area (crowding) for apoptosis.
papers.conclusion: Virtual perturbation is a straightforward technique for assessing the impact of input features on model outputs and can be used to generate hypotheses for physical experimentation, confirming that the model has learned the known biological mechanism.
papers.key_findings:
Virtual perturbations to PC1 (nuclear area) produce predictable, monotonic effects on the model's predictions: increasing PC1 decreases mitosis and increases apoptosis predictions within the realistic range.
Switching the cell type of neighboring cells has minimal effect on predictions, confirming that neighbor cell type is not an important determinant of cell fate.
The method is robust across multiple models trained with cross-validation, suggesting the learned relationship is consistent.
Perturbations that push the data out-of-distribution lead to synthetic predictions, indicating the model's sensitivity to OOD data.
The technique can be applied to any context (audio, text, etc.) and does not require assumptions about the downstream model.
papers.limitation:
Perturbations can move the data out-of-distribution (OOD), and DNNs trained on a specific distribution may not perform well OOD, limiting the scientific value of such perturbations.
The method depends on having a disentangled representation to associate latent features with specific physical/conceptual attributes.
future_direction: Explore the concept of the Rashomon set more rigorously to discover properties common to all members of the equal-performance function set.
Use virtual perturbation to generate hypotheses for physical experimentation, allowing researchers to rapidly explore the space of possible experiments.
Apply perturbations for varying lengths of time to investigate whether apoptosis is dependent on the duration of crowding as well as its severity.
papers.abstract: Explainable deep learning holds significant promise in extracting scientific insights from experimental observations. This is especially so in the field of bio-imaging, where the raw data is often voluminous, yet extremely variable and difficult to study. However, one persistent challenge in deep learning assisted scientific discovery is that the workings of artificial neural networks are often difficult to interpret. Here we present a simple technique for investigating the behaviour of trained neural networks: virtual perturbation. By making precise and systematic alterations to input data or internal representations thereof, we are able to discover causal relationships in the outputs of a deep learning model, and by extension, in the underlying phenomenon itself. As an exemplar, we use our recently described deep-learning based cell fate prediction model. We trained the network to predict the fate of less fit cells in an experimental model of mechanical cell competition. By applying virtual perturbation to the trained network, we discover causal relationships between a cell’s environment and eventual fate. We compare these with known properties of the biological system under investigation to demonstrate that the model faithfully captures insights previously established by experimental research.

papers.title: Emergent World Representations: Exploring a Sequence Model Trained on a Synthetic Task
papers.research_question: Does a sequence model trained on a synthetic task (Othello game transcripts) learn an internal representation of the board state, and is that representation causal to its predictions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides evidence that a GPT model trained on Othello game transcripts learns a nonlinear internal representation of the board state, which is causally involved in its predictions. It introduces intervention techniques and latent saliency maps for interpretability.
papers.conclusion: The experiments provide evidence that Othello-GPT maintains a nonlinear internal representation of the game board state, which is causally linked to its predictions. The tools introduced (nonlinear probes, interventions, latent saliency maps) may prove useful for interpretability in natural language settings.
papers.key_findings:
Othello-GPT predicts legal moves with high accuracy, and this is not due to memorization.
Nonlinear probes can accurately decode the board state from internal activations, while linear probes perform poorly.
Intervention experiments show that the board representation is causal to the model's predictions.
Latent saliency maps reveal differences between models trained on synthetic vs. championship data, indicating different learned strategies.
The internal representation of the board state is nonlinear and emerges during training.
papers.limitation: Latent saliency maps only attribute to one tile when multiple tiles are involved in a move, which does not fully capture the Othello rule logic.
future_direction: Extend investigation to other, more complex games.
Compare strategies learned by a sequence model with those of a model trained with a priori knowledge of Othello.
Study how results generalize to natural language models.
papers.abstract: Language models show a surprising range of capabilities, but the source of their apparent competence is unclear. Do these networks just memorize a collection of surface statistics, or do they rely on internal representations of the process that generates the sequences they see? We investigate this question by applying a variant of the GPT model to the task of predicting legal moves in a simple board game, Othello. Although the network has no a priori knowledge of the game or its rules, we uncover evidence of an emergent nonlinear internal representation of the board state. Interventional experiments indicate this representation can be used to control the output of the network and create "latent saliency maps" that can help explain predictions in human terms.

papers.title: Understanding Representation Dynamics of Diffusion Models via Low-Dimensional Modeling
papers.research_question: What causes the unimodal representation dynamics in diffusion models, and how does it relate to model generalization?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a theoretical explanation for the unimodal representation dynamics in diffusion models, showing it arises from capturing the low-dimensional data structure, and empirically demonstrates that this dynamics indicates model generalization.
papers.conclusion: The unimodal representation dynamics in diffusion models arise from successful capture of low-dimensional data distributions and serve as a reliable indicator of model generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Unimodal representation dynamics emerge when diffusion models successfully capture the underlying low-dimensional data distribution.
The dynamics are driven by an interplay between denoising strength and class confidence across noise levels.
The presence of unimodal dynamics reliably predicts generalization in classification tasks, while memorization leads to monotonic dynamics.
The unimodal pattern becomes less obvious with smaller dataset sizes and transitions to a monotonically decreasing curve in the memorization regime.
Early stopping during training can improve generalization and restore unimodal dynamics in limited data regimes.
papers.abstract: Diffusion models, though originally designed for generative tasks, have demonstrated impressive self-supervised representation learning capabilities. A particularly intriguing phenomenon in these models is the emergence of unimodal representation dynamics, where the quality of learned features peaks at an intermediate noise level. In this work, we conduct a comprehensive theoretical and empirical investigation of this phenomenon. Leveraging the inherent low-dimensionality structure of image data, we theoretically demonstrate that the unimodal dynamic emerges when the diffusion model successfully captures the underlying data distribution. The unimodality arises from an interplay between denoising strength and class confidence across noise scales. Empirically, we further show that, in classification tasks, the presence of unimodal dynamics reliably reflects the generalization of the diffusion model: it emerges when the model generates novel images and gradually transitions to a monotonically decreasing curve as the model begins to memorize the training data.

papers.title: Modelling Cellular Perturbations with the Sparse Additive Mechanism Shift Variational Autoencoder
papers.research_question: How to model the effects of diverse interventions on cells to characterize unknown biological mechanisms of action, combining compositionality, disentanglement, and interpretability for perturbation models?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SAMS-VAE, a generative model that combines sparsity, compositionality, and disentanglement for perturbation modeling, demonstrating improved predictive performance and interpretability on single-cell sequencing data.
papers.conclusion: SAMS-VAE is a useful model for perturbational screening data, with improved predictive performance and ability to recover factors correlated with biological mechanisms, and may aid in scientific discovery.
papers.key_findings:
SAMS-VAE with correlated inference achieves the best test IWELBO and average treatment effect correlation.
SAMS-VAE's latent mask is more predictive of annotated biological pathways than SVAE+.
SAMS-VAE and CPA-VAE perform well on out-of-distribution combinatorial tasks and in low-data settings.
SAMS-VAE improves prediction of nonlinear genetic interactions over a naive linear model.
Correlated inference strategies (correlated zbasal and correlated E) improve model performance.
papers.limitation: The prior on the mask may not enforce sparsity as desired when sample size increases, requiring adjustment of the prior strength to achieve desired sparsity.
future_direction: Studying how perturbations interact and compose in more complex fashion.
Incorporating different forms of prior knowledge into such systems.
papers.abstract: Generative models of observations under interventions have been a vibrant topic of interest across machine learning and the sciences in recent years. For example, in drug discovery, there is a need to model the effects of diverse interventions on cells in order to characterize unknown biological mechanisms of action. We propose the Sparse Additive Mechanism Shift Variational Autoencoder, SAMS-VAE, to combine compositionality, disentanglement, and interpretability for perturbation models. SAMS-VAE models the latent state of a perturbed sample as the sum of a local latent variable capturing sample-specific variation and sparse global variables of latent intervention effects. Crucially, SAMS-VAE sparsifies these global latent variables for individual perturbations to identify disentangled, perturbation-specific latent subspaces that are flexibly composable. We evaluate SAMS-VAE both quantitatively and qualitatively on a range of tasks using two popular single cell sequencing datasets. In order to measure perturbation-specific model-properties, we also introduce a framework for evaluation of perturbation models based on average treatment effects with links to posterior predictive checks. SAMS-VAE outperforms comparable models in terms of generalization across in-distribution and out-of-distribution tasks, including a combinatorial reasoning task under resource paucity, and yields interpretable latent structures which correlate strongly to known biological mechanisms. Our results suggest SAMS-VAE is an interesting addition to the modeling toolkit for machine learning-driven scientific discovery.

papers.title: Can sparse autoencoders make sense of gene expression latent variable models?
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders (SAEs) be effectively used to interpret latent representations in biological data, specifically single-cell gene expression data?
papers.core_contribution: This work explores the potential of sparse autoencoders (SAEs) for interpreting latent representations in biological data, introduces scFeatureLens for automated annotation of SAE features with biological concepts, and demonstrates that SAEs can extract meaningful features that steer cells into desired biological programs.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that SAEs are a valuable tool for interpreting latent representations in biological data, and the introduced scFeatureLens pipeline provides a scalable framework for improved interpretability in single-cell analysis, though more research is needed in this field.
papers.key_findings:
Distribution type and distance of hidden generative variables affect their recovery from latent representations.
SAEs can extract meaningful features from single-cell expression models that successfully steer cells into desired programs, with features acting either locally or globally.
SAEs can uncover subtle biological signals that might otherwise be missed in traditional analysis.
The introduced automated pipeline, scFeatureLens, enables large-scale interpretability analysis by linking SAE features to biological concepts from gene sets.
SAEs do not provide an advantage over simple baselines for recovering known features, but are valuable for discovering unknown features and data generation structure.
papers.limitation:
Variables with an indirect effect on the observed data and little structure in the generative process could practically not be recovered.
SAEs do not pose an advantage in the recovery of known or hypothesized features compared to simple baselines.
The case study was limited to Gene Ontology terms which are incomplete and biased towards well-studied genes.
future_direction: Future work could explore metrics for evaluating the biological meaningfulness in and differences between embeddings.
More research is needed in the field of interpretability for biological models.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have lately been used to uncover interpretable latent features in large language models. By projecting dense embeddings into a much higher-dimensional and sparse space, learned features become disentangled and easier to interpret. This work explores the potential of SAEs for decomposing embeddings in complex and high-dimensional biological data. Using simulated data, it outlines the efficacy, hyperparameter landscape, and limitations of SAEs when it comes to extracting ground truth generative variables from latent space. The application to embeddings from pretrained single-cell models shows that SAEs can find and steer key biological processes and even uncover subtle biological signals that might otherwise be missed. This work further introduces scFeatureLens, an automated interpretability approach for linking SAE features and biological concepts from gene sets to enable large-scale analysis and hypothesis generation in single-cell gene expression models.

papers.title: Probing the Relationship Between Latent Linear Dynamical Systems and Low-Rank Recurrent Neural Network Models
papers.research_question: When can latent linear dynamical system (LDS) models be converted to low-rank linear recurrent neural network (RNN) models, and vice versa?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that latent LDS models are non-Markovian and cannot generally be converted to low-rank linear RNNs, but can be approximated by RNNs in specific limits (e.g., large number of neurons, orthogonal observation noise). Conversely, any linear low-rank RNN can be mapped to a latent LDS model with latent dimensionality at most twice the rank of the RNN.
papers.conclusion: The paper establishes the mathematical relationship between latent LDS and low-rank linear RNN models, showing their equivalence in limit cases and providing mappings between them, which opens the door to comparing different fitting approaches and developing new inference methods.
papers.key_findings:
Latent LDS models generate non-Markovian observation sequences, while low-rank linear RNNs are strictly Markovian.
A latent LDS can be approximated by a low-rank linear RNN that matches its first-order marginals, with the approximation becoming exact when the observation noise is orthogonal to the latent subspace or in the limit of a large number of neurons relative to the latent dimensionality.
Any linear low-rank RNN can be converted to an equivalent latent LDS model, with the latent space dimension at most twice the rank of the RNN's connectivity matrix.
The two model classes are closely related, with linear low-rank RNNs comprising a subset of the broader class of latent LDS models.
The relationship provides a foundation for comparing different fitting approaches for these models and for developing probabilistic methods to infer RNN parameters from data.
papers.limitation: The analysis is limited to linear models.
future_direction: Developing probabilistic methods for inferring RNN parameters from data by leveraging the relationship with LDS models.
Relating switching LDS models to local linear approximations of non-linear low-rank RNNs.
papers.abstract: A large body of work has suggested that neural populations exhibit low-dimensional dynamics during behavior. However, there are a variety of different approaches for modeling low-dimensional neural population activity. One approach involves latent linear dynamical system (LDS) models, in which population activity is described by a projection of low-dimensional latent variables with linear dynamics. A second approach involves low-rank recurrent neural networks (RNNs), in which population activity arises directly from a low-dimensional projection of past activity. Although these two modeling approaches have strong similarities, they arise in different contexts and tend to have different domains of application. Here we examine the precise relationship between latent LDS models and linear low-rank RNNs. When can one model class be converted to the other, and vice versa? We show that latent LDS models can only be converted to RNNs in specific limit cases, due to the non-Markovian property of latent LDS models. Conversely, we show that linear RNNs can be mapped onto LDS models, with latent dimensionality at most twice the rank of the RNN. A surprising consequence of our results is that a partially observed RNN is better represented by an LDS model than by an RNN consisting of only observed units.

papers.title: The cell as a token: high-dimensional geometry in language models and cell embeddings
papers.research_question: How can advances in understanding the geometry of language model embeddings inform the analysis of single-cell genomics data?
papers.core_contribution: This review highlights how principles from language model embeddings, such as context-dependence and low-dimensional manifolds, can guide the development and interpretation of single-cell foundation models.
papers.conclusion: Drawing parallels between language models and single-cell embeddings reveals shared principles in high-dimensional geometry, but biological context is more complex, requiring future models to integrate multimodal data and address dynamical processes.
papers.key_findings:
The distributional hypothesis in language, which links word meaning to context, can be analogously applied to single-cell data for self-supervised learning of cell embeddings.
Low-dimensional manifolds in embedding spaces capture semantic relationships in language and developmental pathways in biology, enabling analogies and trajectory inference.
Dynamic embeddings that incorporate context, such as through self-attention in language models or spatial data in cells, improve representation fidelity and disambiguation.
Interpretability methods like linear probes and sparse autoencoders, used in language models, can be adapted to analyze internal representations in single-cell foundation models for feature identification.
The analogy between cells and tokens has limitations due to the ordered, discrete nature of language context versus the multiscale, indirect context of biological systems.
papers.limitation: Biological context is multiscale, incomplete, and indirect compared to the discrete, ordered sequences in language, limiting direct analogies.
future_direction: Integrating diverse experimental contexts and multimodal data without loss of biological specificity in cell embeddings.
Developing improved benchmarks to test the ability of foundation models to parse complex and indirect regulatory logic in biology.
Creating temporally aware embedding models that capture continuous trajectories and causal relationships in dynamical biological systems.
papers.abstract: Single-cell sequencing technology maps cells to a high-dimensional space encoding their internal activity. Recently-proposed virtual cell models extend this concept, enriching cells' representations based on patterns learned from pretraining on vast cell atlases. This review explores how advances in understanding the structure of natural language embeddings informs ongoing efforts to analyze single-cell datasets. Both fields process unstructured data by partitioning datasets into tokens embedded within a high-dimensional vector space. We discuss how the context of tokens influences the geometry of embedding space, and how low-dimensional manifolds shape this space's robustness and interpretation. We highlight how new developments in foundation models for language, such as interpretability probes and in-context reasoning, can inform efforts to construct cell atlases and train virtual cell models.

papers.title: A Spatiotemporal Perspective on Dynamical Computation in Neural Information Processing Systems
papers.research_question: What is the functional role of spatiotemporal flows (e.g., traveling waves) in neural systems, and are they necessary for processing signals that undergo flow transformations like motion?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a theoretical framework that formalizes the connection between 'motion' and flowing neural dynamics (e.g., traveling waves) through the lens of equivariant neural network theory, arguing that such recurrent spatiotemporal dynamics are necessary for accurate and stable processing of any signal undergoing a flow transformation.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that spatiotemporal dynamics, particularly traveling waves, are fundamental for neural computation in a dynamic world, serving as an innate inductive bias that enables efficient and generalizable processing of signals undergoing flow transformations, thereby unifying a wide range of observations in neuroscience and machine learning.
papers.key_findings:
Traveling waves and similar spatiotemporal dynamics are not merely epiphenomena but are necessary for recurrent neural networks to achieve flow equivariance—i.e., to process moving inputs in a manner that is equivalent to processing stationary inputs with a corresponding flow applied to the hidden state.
Flow equivariance provides a normative explanation for why biological neural systems exhibit traveling waves: given biological constraints like conduction delays and metabolic costs, local spatiotemporal flows are the most natural realization of latent flows required for equivariant computation.
The framework generalizes 'motion' to flows in abstract representational spaces, showing how flow equivariance can underpin structured memory formation, cognitive maps, and logical reasoning by mirroring unobserved world-state transformations.
This spatiotemporal perspective reconciles the observed prevalence of traveling waves in neural recordings with classical feature-detector accounts, embedding selectivity within a broader dynamical framework that is optimized for a world dominated by structured transformations over space and time.
The theory predicts that artificial neural networks built with flow-equivariant inductive biases (e.g., locally coupled oscillatory recurrent networks) should exhibit improved data efficiency and generalization on tasks involving spatiotemporally structured inputs.
future_direction: Experimental testing of the predictions derived from the flow-equivariance framework in both biological and artificial neural systems.
Development of novel neural network architectures that explicitly incorporate flow-equivariant principles to improve performance on video, navigation, and memory tasks.
Further theoretical work to extend the framework to more complex, non-commutative flows and to integrate it with other principles of efficient coding and learning.
papers.abstract: Spatiotemporal flows of neural activity, such as traveling waves, have been observed throughout the brain since the earliest recordings; yet there is still little consensus on their functional role. Recent experiments and models have linked traveling waves to visual and physical motion, but these observations have been difficult to reconcile with standard accounts of topographically organized selectivity and feedforward receptive fields. Here, we introduce a theoretical framework that formalizes and generalizes the connection between 'motion' and flowing neural dynamics in the language of equivariant neural network theory. We consider 'motion' not only in physical or visual spaces, but also in more abstract representational spaces, and we argue that recurrent traveling-wave-like dynamics are not just useful but necessary for accurate and stable processing of any signal undergoing such motion. Formally, we show that for any non-trivial recurrent neural network to process a sequence undergoing a flow transformation (such as visual motion) in a structured equivariant manner, its hidden state dynamics must actively realize a homomorphic representation of the same flow through recurrent connectivity. In this ''spatiotemporal perspective on dynamical computation'', traveling waves and related flows are best understood as faithful dynamic representations of stimulus flows; and consequently the natural inclination of biological systems towards such dynamics may be viewed as an innate inductive bias towards efficiency and generalization in the spatiotemporally-structured dynamical world they inhabit.

papers.title: State Space Models Naturally Produce Time Cell and Oscillatory Behaviors and Scale to Abstract Cognitive Functions
papers.research_question: How do State Space Models (SSMs) produce time cell and oscillatory behaviors, and can they scale to abstract cognitive functions? The paper investigates whether these behaviors arise from learning or from pre-configured network structures.
papers.core_contribution: State Space Models (SSMs) with HiPPO initialization naturally produce time cell and oscillatory behaviors, and learning primarily acts as a selection mechanism that fine-tunes pre-configured oscillatory modes rather than constructing temporal codes from scratch.
papers.conclusion: Rotational dynamics in State Space Models provide a computationally tractable framework for temporal cognition, suggesting that pre-configured basis functions are key to generating time cells and other temporal codes observed in neural circuits.
papers.key_findings:
HiPPO-initialized SSMs exhibit time cell and ramping cell behaviors even before training, while randomly initialized networks do not.
Learning in HiPPO-initialized SSMs primarily involves reconfiguring the readout layer (C), with minimal changes to the internal state dynamics (Λ and B).
The model can adapt to extended delays (retiming) by retraining only the readout layer, while randomly initialized networks fail to adapt.
The model can perform abstract lap-counting, with lap count information being linearly separable in the hidden state space.
The diverse temporal profiles (time cells, ramping cells) emerge from the projection of underlying rotational dynamics in the complex plane onto the real axis.
papers.limitation:
The complexity of the tasks employed may not fully exploit the model's capacity, as randomly initialized networks also achieved high accuracy.
HiPPO initialization is one of a class of suitable initializations, and there is no guarantee the brain uses this specific orthogonal basis.
The model abstracts away the intricate microarchitecture of biological circuits, such as complex connectivity and diverse cell types.
future_direction: Investigate whether evolving a population of SSMs over generations, selecting for memory capacity, causes weight matrices to converge toward HiPPO-like structures.
Systematically quantify the spectrum of learned rotational frequencies and compare them to biological oscillation bands (e.g., theta, gamma).
Validate the framework using real spiking data to test robustness amidst the sparsity and stochasticity of neural substrates.
papers.abstract: A grand challenge in modern neuroscience is to bridge the gap between the detailed mapping of microscale neural circuits and mechanistic understanding of cognitive functions. While extensive knowledge exists about neuronal connectivity and biophysics, how these low-level phenomena eventually produce abstract behaviors remains largely unresolved. Here, we propose that a model based on State Space Models, an emerging class of deep learning architectures, can be a potential biological model for analysis. We suggest that the differential equations governing elements in a State Space Model are conceptually consistent with the dynamics of biophysical processes, while the model offers a scalable framework to build on the dynamics to produce emergent behaviors observed in experimental neuroscience. We test this model by training a network employing a diagonal state transition matrix on temporal discrimination tasks with reinforcement learning. Our results suggest that neural behaviors such as time cells naturally emerge from two fundamental principles: optimal pre-configuration and rotational dynamics. These features are shown mathematically to optimize history compression, and naturally generate structured temporal dynamics even prior to training, mirroring recent findings in biological circuits. We show that learning acts primarily as a selection mechanism that fine-tunes these pre-configured oscillatory modes, rather than constructing temporal codes de novo. The model can be readily scaled to abstract cognitive functions such as event counting, supporting the use of State Space Models as a computationally tractable framework for understanding neural activities.

papers.title: Unconditional CNN denoisers contain sparse semantic representation of images
papers.research_question: How does an unconditional denoising network internally represent images, and what semantic information does this representation capture?
papers.core_contribution: Unconditional denoising networks learn a sparse semantic representation in the middle block, where spatial averages of channels form a representation vector that captures semantic similarity between images.
papers.conclusion: A network trained solely with a denoising objective, without any external conditioning, learns a rich and accessible representation of image structure.
papers.key_findings:
The middle block of a UNet denoiser decomposes images into sparse subsets of active channels, and their spatial averages form a stable representation vector.
Channels in the middle block are either selective (responding to specific patterns) or non-selective (common patterns).
Euclidean distances in the representation space correspond to semantic similarity between images.
Clustering the representation vectors yields semantically coherent groups that are only partially aligned with object classes.
A stochastic reconstruction algorithm can generate images conditioned on the representation, revealing the features captured.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to fully convolutional UNets and it is unclear if similar representations arise in other architectures like transformers.
The geometry of the representation space (union of subspaces) is not fully characterized.
future_direction: Deeper understanding of the geometry of the representation space, including the distribution of dimensionalities of subspaces.
Investigating the role of encoder and decoder blocks and their interaction with noise level.
Examining whether similar representations arise in more modern architectures such as transformers.
papers.abstract: Generative diffusion models learn probability densities over diverse image datasets by estimating the score with a neural network trained to remove noise. Despite their remarkable success in generating high-quality images, the internal mechanisms of the underlying score networks are not well understood. Here, we examine the image representation that arises from score estimation in a {fully-convolutional unconditional UNet}. We show that the middle block of the UNet decomposes individual images into sparse subsets of active channels, and that the vector of spatial averages of these channels can provide a nonlinear representation of the underlying clean images. Euclidean distances in this representation space are semantically meaningful, even though no conditioning information is provided during training. We develop a novel algorithm for stochastic reconstruction of images conditioned on this representation: The synthesis using the unconditional model is "self-guided" by the representation extracted from that very same model. For a given representation, the common patterns in the set of reconstructed samples reveal the features captured in the middle block of the UNet. Together, these results show, for the first time, that a measure of semantic similarity emerges, unsupervised, solely from the denoising objective.

papers.title: How 'Neural' is a Neural Foundation Model?
papers.research_question: Do neural decoding and encoding manifolds reveal new insights into how foundation models represent temporal response patterns? Are their representations brain-like?
papers.core_contribution: The recurrent module of the neural foundation model shows brain-like representational properties, while the feedforward encoder and readout module have limitations; design changes are suggested for better biological alignment.
papers.conclusion: The FNN is only a partial digital twin of the mouse visual system; its recurrent module is most brain-like, but design improvements in early recurrence and readout constraints could enhance biological alignment.
papers.key_findings:
The recurrent module achieves the highest stimulus separability and closest alignment with biological visual cortex.
The feedforward encoder lacks biologically plausible temporal patterns and contains non-selective neurons.
The readout module uses numerous specialized feature maps rather than biologically plausible mechanisms.
Decoding trajectories in the recurrent stage show tubular structure but fewer crossings than biological data, indicating less complex dynamics.
Encoding manifolds reveal that the FNN's neuronal organization, especially in the readout, is clustered by feature maps and differs from the continuous topology of biological cortex.
papers.limitation:
The FNN does not fully capture the complexity of neural dynamics, as evidenced by fewer crossings in decoding trajectories compared to biological data.
The readout module's highly clustered, feature-map-based organization is not brain-like.
future_direction: Introduce recurrence in early encoder stages.
Constraining features in the readout module to be more biologically plausible.
Investigate more complex temporal processing to better match biological dynamics.
papers.abstract: Foundation models have shown remarkable success in fitting biological visual systems; however, their black-box nature inherently limits their utility for understanding brain function. Here, we peek inside a SOTA foundation model of neural activity (Wang et al., 2025) as a physiologist might, characterizing each 'neuron' based on its temporal response properties to parametric stimuli. We analyze how different stimuli are represented in neural activity space by building decoding manifolds, and we analyze how different neurons are represented in stimulus-response space by building neural encoding manifolds. We find that the different processing stages of the model (i.e., the feedforward encoder, recurrent, and readout modules) each exhibit qualitatively different representational structures in these manifolds. The recurrent module shows a jump in capabilities over the encoder module by 'pushing apart' the representations of different temporal stimulus patterns. Our 'tubularity' metric quantifies this stimulus-dependent development of neural activity as biologically plausible. The readout module achieves high fidelity by using numerous specialized feature maps rather than biologically plausible mechanisms. Overall, this study provides a window into the inner workings of a prominent neural foundation model, gaining insights into the biological relevance of its internals through the novel analysis of its neurons' joint temporal response patterns. Our findings suggest design changes that could bring neural foundation models into closer alignment with biological systems: introducing recurrence in early encoder stages, and constraining features in the readout module.

papers.title: CytoSAE: Interpretable Cell Embeddings for Hematology
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders be applied for interpretable morphological concept discovery in hematological imaging?
papers.core_contribution: CytoSAE is a sparse autoencoder that discovers interpretable morphological concepts in hematological images, generalizes across diverse and out-of-domain datasets, and enables explainable disease classification at patch, image, patient, and disease levels.
papers.conclusion: CytoSAE successfully learns interpretable morphological features across different hematological datasets, maintains generalizability to out-of-domain data, and enables multi-level analysis for interpretable disease classification.
papers.key_findings:
CytoSAE discovers morphologically relevant concepts that generalize across peripheral blood and bone marrow cytology datasets, validated by medical experts.
Patch-wise attribution allows sub-cellular level analysis of concepts, highlighting consistent morphological features across datasets.
Patient-level concept barcodes reveal disease-specific morphological features for AML subtypes, such as monocytic precursors for CBFB::MYH11 and granulated blasts for PML::RARA.
CytoSAE concepts achieve multi-class classification performance comparable to state-of-the-art deep learning methods while providing explainability.
Ablation studies show the number of discovered concepts is stable across expansion factors and hyperparameters, with optimal layers between 7–11 for concept balance.
papers.limitation: Manual expert validation was conducted only at the dataset level, not per patient, to avoid human selection bias in concept discovery.
future_direction: Explore patient-specific concept retrieval while minimizing subjectivity.
Incorporate semi-supervised learning techniques to refine the discovered features further.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) emerged as a promising tool for mechanistic interpretability of transformer-based foundation models. Very recently, SAEs were also adopted for the visual domain, enabling the discovery of visual concepts and their patch-wise attribution to tokens in the transformer model.
