papers.core_contribution: Pre-training neural networks on retinal waves improves performance on spatial translation tasks and leads to more linearly separable feature representations, as explained by manifold geometry.
papers.conclusion: Retinal waves can instruct the formation of visual representations that support object recognition, and their spatiotemporal properties prepare networks for higher-order feature extraction.
papers.key_findings:
Pre-training on retinal waves significantly improves performance on spatial translation tasks, while slightly improving image classification and color change tasks.
Networks pre-trained on retinal waves show increased separability (capacity) of object manifolds for spatial translation, with decreased manifold dimension and radius.
Pre-training reduces inter-manifold correlations and maintains an effective dimensionality of the feature space, avoiding vanishing or exploding dimensionality.
The spatiotemporal characteristics of retinal waves are necessary for learning spatial invariance; shuffling spatial or temporal structure reduces performance.
Real and simulated retinal waves yield similar results, suggesting common spatiotemporal features drive the effects.
papers.limitation:
Findings are subject to the choice of network architecture (ResNet-18), learning algorithm (SimCLR), and dataset (postnatal mouse retinal waves).
Retinal waves are not the only form of spontaneous activity during development.
future_direction: Consider the role of cortical feedback and introduce bioplausible, synaptically local learning rules.
Investigate the role of spontaneous activity in other modalities like temporal prediction.
Perform laboratory experiments in mice to verify model predictions and study neural object manifolds at the onset of vision.
papers.abstract: Prior to the onset of vision, neurons in the developing mammalian retina spontaneously fire in correlated activity patterns known as retinal waves. Experimental evidence suggests that retinal waves strongly influence the emergence of sensory representations before visual experience. We aim to model this early stage of functional development by using movies of neurally active developing retinas as pre-training data for neural networks. Specifically, we pre-train a ResNet-18 with an unsupervised contrastive learning objective (SimCLR) on both simulated and experimentally-obtained movies of retinal waves, then evaluate its performance on image classification tasks. We find that pre-training on retinal waves significantly improves performance on tasks that test object invariance to spatial translation, while slightly improving performance on more complex tasks like image classification. Notably, these performance boosts are realized on held-out natural images even though the pre-training procedure does not include any natural image data. We then propose a geometrical explanation for the increase in network performance, namely that the spatiotemporal characteristics of retinal waves facilitate the formation of separable feature representations. In particular, we demonstrate that networks pre-trained on retinal waves are more effective at separating image manifolds than randomly initialized networks, especially for manifolds defined by sets of spatial translations. These findings indicate that the broad spatiotemporal properties of retinal waves prepare networks for higher order feature extraction.

papers.title: exBERT: A Visual Analysis Tool to Explore Learned Representations in Transformer Models
papers.research_question: How can we develop an interactive tool to explore learned representations and attentions in Transformer models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces EXBERT, an interactive visualization tool for exploring learned representations and attentions in Transformer models, enabling hypothesis formulation and replication of prior analyses.
papers.conclusion: EXBERT is a tool that provides interactive insights into Transformer models' representations and attentions, facilitating hypothesis generation and analysis.
papers.key_findings:
EXBERT can replicate prior findings on BERT's attention heads learning linguistic dependencies such as AUX and POBJ.
BERT's embeddings encode linguistic information progressively across layers, with verbs becoming more prominent in later layers.
EXBERT detects gender bias in GPT-2 by showing that it predicts gendered pronouns based on stereotypical associations.
GPT-2's attention heads learn syntactic structures like AUX and DOBJ dependencies, similar to BERT.
The tool allows for interactive exploration and quick hypothesis testing of model behavior through attention visualization and corpus similarity search.
papers.limitation: EXBERT only presents statistics across a small number of neighbors for a single token at a time, which may not reveal global model behavior.
papers.abstract: Large Transformer-based language models can route and reshape complex information via their multi-headed attention mechanism. Although the attention never receives explicit supervision, it can exhibit recognizable patterns following linguistic or positional information. Analyzing the learned representations and attentions is paramount to furthering our understanding of the inner workings of these models. However, analyses have to catch up with the rapid release of new models and the growing diversity of investigation techniques. To support analysis for a wide variety of models, we introduce EXBERT, a tool to help humans conduct flexible, interactive investigations and formulate hypotheses for the model-internal reasoning process. EXBERT provides insights into the meaning of the contextual representations and attention by matching a humanspecified input to similar contexts in large annotated datasets. By aggregating the annotations of the matched contexts, EXBERT can quickly replicate findings from literature and extend them to previously not analyzed models.

papers.title: Mechanistic Independence: A Principle for Identifiable Disentangled Representations
papers.research_question: Under what conditions can disentangled representations be identified without relying on statistical assumptions, by using mechanistic independence criteria?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a unified framework for disentangled representations based on mechanistic independence, proposing several independence criteria and proving identifiability theorems for latent subspaces under nonlinear, non-invertible mixing.
papers.conclusion: Mechanistic independence provides a unifying framework that clarifies the conditions for identifiability of disentangled representations without relying on statistical assumptions.
papers.key_findings:
Local disentanglement implies global disentanglement under mild topological conditions (path-connectedness and local injectivity).
Type D independence (disjoint support) yields identifiability of latent subspaces up to block-wise invertible transforms and permutations.
Type M independence (mutual non-inclusion) yields identifiability when combined with a sparsity regularizer.
Type S independence (sparsity gap) yields identifiability even when supports overlap.
Type Hn independence (vanishing cross-derivatives) yields identifiability when the generator is separable of order n.
papers.limitation: The sparsity gap condition (Type S) is intractable to optimize in practice, and finding robust surrogate losses is an open problem.
future_direction: Identifying robust surrogate losses for the sparsity gap condition (Type S).
papers.abstract: Disentangled representations seek to recover latent factors of variation underlying observed data, yet their identifiability is still not fully understood. We introduce a unified framework in which disentanglement is achieved through mechanistic independence, which characterizes latent factors by how they act on observed variables rather than by their latent distribution. This perspective is invariant to changes of the latent density, even when such changes induce statistical dependencies among factors. Within this framework, we propose several related independence criteria -- ranging from support-based and sparsity-based to higher-order conditions -- and show that each yields identifiability of latent subspaces, even under nonlinear, non-invertible mixing. We further establish a hierarchy among these criteria and provide a graph-theoretic characterization of latent subspaces as connected components. Together, these results clarify the conditions under which disentangled representations can be identified without relying on statistical assumptions.

papers.title: Consequences of Slow Neural Dynamics for Incremental Learning
papers.research_question: How does the temporal smoothness of internal states affect the efficiency of learning when the training data are also temporally smooth? How does it affect the kinds of representations that are learned?
papers.core_contribution: Networks with linear recurrence and gating learn more efficiently from temporally correlated data and can learn internal representations that separate fast and slow sources in the environment.
papers.conclusion: Intrinsic temporal autocorrelation is not an obstacle for learning but can be an inductive bias that accelerates learning and leads to more interpretable, timescale-separated representations when learning from correlated data streams.
papers.key_findings:
Feedforward networks learn slower with temporally autocorrelated data, while networks with linear recurrence learn faster.
Adding a gating mechanism to reset memory at category transitions allows recurrent networks to benefit from autocorrelation while avoiding interference from unrelated prior information.
Networks with recurrence and multiscale gating can learn internal representations that un-mix features varying on different timescales from multi-scale autocorrelated data.
The linear-recurrence-plus-gating model generalizes better across different levels of temporal autocorrelation compared to an LSTM trained with backpropagation through time.
Intrinsic temporal autocorrelation in neural dynamics can serve as a useful inductive bias for incremental learning from correlated data.
papers.limitation:
The gating mechanism in the autoencoder experiments is somewhat artificial as it requires knowing which features change quickly or slowly.
The work uses simple architectures and synthetic datasets; future work should test on larger architectures and more realistic datasets.
future_direction: Examine the efficacy of linear recurrence and gating mechanisms in CNN architectures trained on video segmentation sequences.
Test whether results generalize to larger architectures and more realistic datasets with a broader hyperparameter search.
Extend the autoencoder architecture to a predictive architecture that predicts the next stimulus rather than reconstructing the present one.
Investigate the broader consequences of learning with recurrence for reducing the difference between human internal representations and those of feedforward nets.
papers.abstract: In the human brain, internal states are often correlated over time (due to local recurrence and other intrinsic circuit properties), punctuated by abrupt transitions. At first glance, temporal smoothness of internal states presents a problem for learning input-output mappings (e.g. category labels for images), because the internal representation of the input will contain a mixture of current input and prior inputs. However, when training with naturalistic data (e.g. movies) there is also temporal autocorrelation in the input. How does the temporal "smoothness" of internal states affect the efficiency of learning when the training data are also temporally smooth? How does it affect the kinds of representations that are learned? We found that, when trained with temporally smooth data, "slow" neural networks (equipped with linear recurrence and gating mechanisms) learned to categorize more efficiently than feedforward networks. Furthermore, networks with linear recurrence and multi-timescale gating could learn internal representations that "un-mixed" quickly-varying and slowly-varying data sources. Together, these findings demonstrate how a fundamental property of cortical dynamics (their temporal autocorrelation) can serve as an inductive bias, leading to more efficient category learning and to the representational separation of fast and slow sources in the environment.

papers.title: Space as Time Through Neuron Position Learning
papers.research_question: What happens when synaptic delays are defined as Euclidean distances between neurons and neuron positions are learned? How does this space-time coupling affect network topology, functional specialization, and efficiency?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a neuron position learning algorithm that couples space and time through delays defined as Euclidean distances, leading to self-organized modular and efficient network structures with functional specialization.
papers.conclusion: Neuron position learning provides a framework for studying space-time coupling in neural networks, leading to biologically plausible structures and offering benefits for neuromorphic hardware.
papers.key_findings:
Neuron positions in the hidden layer correlate with input connectivity patterns, enabling prediction of positions from weights.
Networks with position learning rely on local computations and form circuits associated with specific tasks.
Under distance-dependent cost regularisation, networks achieve higher modularity and more efficient wiring.
Unconstrained position learning converges on solutions with more local connections, making them robust to pruning of long delays.
Position learning reduces the number of free parameters compared to direct delay learning while maintaining performance.
papers.limitation:
The study focuses on small networks, which may not reflect scaling behavior.
Neurons can be arbitrarily close, unlike biological volume exclusion, which could be addressed by adding repulsive forces.
future_direction: Introduce repulsive forces between neurons to prevent arbitrary closeness.
Extend analysis to modular tasks with added temporal structure, multimodal settings, or multi-task problems.
Combine position learning with structural plasticity algorithms like DEEP R to yield interesting network geometries.
papers.abstract: Biological neural networks exist in physical space where distance influences communication delays: a fundamental coupling between space and time absent in most artificial neural networks. While recent work has separately explored spatial embeddings and learnable synaptic delays in spiking neural networks, we unify these approaches through a novel neuron position learning algorithm where delays relate to the Euclidean distances between neurons. We derive gradients with respect to neuron positions and demonstrate that this biologically-motivated constraint acts as an inductive bias: networks trained on temporal classification tasks spontaneously self-organize into local, clustered topologies and a modular, efficiently wired structure emerges if connection costs are distance-dependent. Remarkably, we observe functional specialization aligned with spatial clustering without explicitly enforcing it. These findings lay the groundwork for networks in which space and time are intrinsically coupled, offering new avenues for mechanistic interpretability, biologically inspired modelling, and efficient implementations.

papers.title: SOM-VAE: Interpretable Discrete Representation Learning on Time Series
papers.research_question: How to learn interpretable discrete representations of time series that are smooth and provide superior clustering performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces SOM-VAE, a framework for learning interpretable discrete representations of time series, featuring a gradient-based self-organizing map and an integrated Markov model for temporal smoothness and improved clustering.
papers.conclusion: SOM-VAE can recover topologically interpretable state representations on time series and static data, improves clustering performance over standard methods, and offers interpretable visualizations that could aid in domains like healthcare.
papers.key_findings:
SOM-VAE outperforms baselines like k-means, VQ-VAE, and traditional SOM in clustering performance on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST in terms of purity and NMI.
The gradient-based SOM training (GB-SOM) performs better than the original SOM algorithm.
The probabilistic Markov model can be learned concurrently with the SOM-VAE and improves clustering performance on noisy data, such as medical time series.
On the chaotic Lorenz system, SOM-VAE learns interpretable representations that capture the macro-states (attractor basins) while ignoring chaotic noise.
On real medical data from the eICU database, SOM-VAE-prob learns representations that are informative for downstream prediction tasks and provides interpretable visualizations of patient trajectories.
future_direction: Extend the probabilistic component for predictions using higher-order Markov Models, Hidden Markov Models, or Gaussian Processes.
Find more theoretically principled ways to overcome the non-differentiability in discrete representation learning.
Learn the neighborhood structure as a graph directly from data instead of fixing a latent space structure like a 2D grid.
papers.abstract: High-dimensional time series are common in many domains. Since human cognition is not optimized to work well in high-dimensional spaces, these areas could benefit from interpretable low-dimensional representations. However, most representation learning algorithms for time series data are difficult to interpret. This is due to non-intuitive mappings from data features to salient properties of the representation and non-smoothness over time. To address this problem, we propose a new representation learning framework building on ideas from interpretable discrete dimensionality reduction and deep generative modeling. This framework allows us to learn discrete representations of time series, which give rise to smooth and interpretable embeddings with superior clustering performance. We introduce a new way to overcome the non-differentiability in discrete representation learning and present a gradient-based version of the traditional self-organizing map algorithm that is more performant than the original. Furthermore, to allow for a probabilistic interpretation of our method, we integrate a Markov model in the representation space. This model uncovers the temporal transition structure, improves clustering performance even further and provides additional explanatory insights as well as a natural representation of uncertainty. We evaluate our model in terms of clustering performance and interpretability on static (Fashion-)MNIST data, a time series of linearly interpolated (Fashion-)MNIST images, a chaotic Lorenz attractor system with two macro states, as well as on a challenging real world medical time series application on the eICU data set. Our learned representations compare favorably with competitor methods and facilitate downstream tasks on the real world data.

papers.title: Towards scientific discovery with dictionary learning: Extracting biological concepts from microscopy foundation models
papers.research_question: Can dictionary learning extract meaningful high-level concepts from unsupervised vision foundation models trained on scientific data (cell microscopy images) where prior knowledge about concepts is limited?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ICFL, a novel sparse dictionary learning algorithm combined with PCA whitening, to successfully extract biologically meaningful concepts (e.g., cell types, genetic perturbations) from frozen representations of vision foundation models trained on cell microscopy images.
papers.conclusion: Dictionary learning, specifically ICFL with PCA whitening, is a powerful and promising approach for extracting interpretable biological concepts from microscopy foundation models, enabling new directions for scientific discovery via mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
ICFL combined with PCA whitening extracts sparse features that correlate with biological concepts such as cell types and genetic perturbations.
ICFL reduces the number of 'dead features' compared to TopK SAEs.
Linear probes on reconstructions from ICFL features preserve significant biological information, with accuracies comparable to probes on original representations.
ICFL features achieve selectivity scores comparable to handcrafted CellProfiler features for identifying genetic perturbations.
Token-level heatmaps from feature directions enable interpretation of subtle morphological changes, such as distinguishing perturbed from control-like cells.
future_direction: Assess whether peak selectivity of handcrafted features can be matched using deep learning-based approaches with fewer non-zero elements.
Future research on interpreting and validating concept directions found in large foundation models for microscopy image data.
papers.abstract: Sparse dictionary learning (DL) has emerged as a powerful approach to extract semantically meaningful concepts from the internals of large language models (LLMs) trained mainly in the text domain. In this work, we explore whether DL can extract meaningful concepts from less human-interpretable scientific data, such as vision foundation models trained on cell microscopy images, where limited prior knowledge exists about which high-level concepts should arise. We propose a novel combination of a sparse DL algorithm, Iterative Codebook Feature Learning (ICFL), with a PCA whitening pre-processing step derived from control data. Using this combined approach, we successfully retrieve biologically meaningful concepts, such as cell types and genetic perturbations. Moreover, we demonstrate how our method reveals subtle morphological changes arising from human-interpretable interventions, offering a promising new direction for scientific discovery via mechanistic interpretability in bioimaging.

papers.title: Transformers learn factored representations
papers.research_question: Do transformers learn to factor their world into parts from next-token prediction, and why would they have an inductive bias for factored representations?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers learn to factor their world into parts, representing each factor in orthogonal subspaces of the residual stream, and show an inductive bias toward factored representations even when it is lossy.
papers.conclusion: Transformers decompose the world into parts and represent them in orthogonal subspaces due to an inductive bias from next-token prediction, suggesting interpretable low-dimensional structure may persist in models trained on complex data.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers learn factored representations in orthogonal subspaces when data has conditionally independent factors.
The dimensionality of activations collapses to the linearly growing factored prediction, not the exponentially growing joint representation.
Factor subspaces become approximately orthogonal over training, as measured by subspace overlap and dimensionality additivity.
Factoring begins at the token embedding layer, with the embedding matrix developing low-rank structure corresponding to factor subspaces.
Transformers exhibit an inductive bias toward factored representations, learning them early even when data is not perfectly factorable, sacrificing fidelity for dimensional efficiency.
papers.limitation: Experiments are conducted on synthetic data with known latent structure, which may not fully capture real-world complexity.
future_direction: Investigate whether differences in factorization behavior between transformers, RNNs, and LSTMs are due to training dynamics or inductive bias.
papers.abstract: Transformers pretrained via next token prediction learn to factor their world into parts, representing these factors in orthogonal subspaces of the residual stream. We formalize two representational hypotheses: (1) a representation in the product space of all factors, whose dimension grows exponentially with the number of parts, or (2) a factored representation in orthogonal subspaces, whose dimension grows linearly. The factored representation is lossless when factors are conditionally independent, but sacrifices predictive fidelity otherwise, creating a tradeoff between dimensional efficiency and accuracy. We derive precise predictions about the geometric structure of activations for each, including the number of subspaces, their dimensionality, and the arrangement of context embeddings within them. We test between these hypotheses on transformers trained on synthetic processes with known latent structure. Models learn factored representations when factors are conditionally independent, and continue to favor them early in training even when noise or hidden dependencies undermine conditional independence, reflecting an inductive bias toward factoring at the cost of fidelity. This provides a principled explanation for why transformers decompose the world into parts, and suggests that interpretable low dimensional structure may persist even in models trained on complex data.

papers.title: What Does BERT Learn about the Structure of Language?
papers.research_question: What linguistic structure does BERT learn? Specifically, can we unveil the representations learned by BERT to proto-linguistics structures?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides evidence that BERT captures hierarchical linguistic structure, with surface features in lower layers, syntactic in middle, and semantic in higher layers, and that it uses deeper layers for long-distance dependencies and implicitly captures tree-like structures.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that BERT captures structural properties of English language, with a hierarchy of linguistic signals and compositional modeling that parallels traditional syntactic analysis.
papers.key_findings:
BERT's phrasal representation captures phrase-level information in the lower layers, which gets diluted in higher layers.
BERT embeds a rich hierarchy of linguistic signals: surface information at the bottom, syntactic in the middle, and semantic at the top.
BERT requires deeper layers to handle long-distance dependency information, such as subject-verb agreement with more attractors.
BERT implicitly implements a tree-based compositional scheme, as shown by Tensor Product Decomposition Networks (TPDN) approximating BERT's representations.
The untrained version of BERT in higher layers outperforms the trained version in predicting sentence length, indicating that training trades off basic surface features for more complex information.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to English and may not generalize to other languages or noisy user-generated content.
future_direction: Investigating if the results transfer to other domains with higher syntactic variability, such as noisy user-generated content or morphologically-rich languages.
papers.abstract: BERT is a recent language representation model that has surprisingly performed well in diverse language understanding benchmarks. This result indicates the possibility that BERT networks capture structural information about language. In this work, we provide novel support for this claim by performing a series of experiments to unpack the elements of English language structure learned by BERT. We first show that BERT's phrasal representation captures phrase-level information in the lower layers. We also show that BERT's intermediate layers encode a rich hierarchy of linguistic information, with surface features at the bottom, syntactic features in the middle and semantic features at the top. BERT turns out to require deeper layers when long-distance dependency information is required, e.g. to track subjectverb agreement. Finally, we show that BERT representations capture linguistic information in a compositional way that mimics classical, tree-like structures.

papers.title: Insights on representational similarity in neural networks with\n canonical correlation
papers.research_question: How can we compare neural network representations and how do they evolve over time?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces projection weighted CCA, an improved method for comparing neural network representations, and uses it to show that generalizing networks converge to more similar representations than memorizing networks, wider networks converge to more similar solutions, and RNNs exhibit bottom-up convergence during training.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates the utility of projection weighted CCA for analyzing neural network representations, revealing insights about convergence and similarity in CNNs and RNNs.
papers.key_findings:
Networks that generalize converge to more similar representations than those that memorize.
Wider networks converge to more similar solutions than narrower networks.
Networks with identical topology but different learning rates converge to distinct clusters of solutions.
RNNs exhibit bottom-up convergence over the course of training.
RNN hidden states vary nonlinearly across sequence timesteps.
future_direction: Examine what is unique about directions preserved across networks trained with different initializations.
Explore whether the insight that similar solutions lead to higher generalization could be used as a regularizer.
Investigate which aspects of RNN representations are stable over time and which vary.
papers.abstract:
Comparing different neural network representations and determining how
representations evolve over time remain challenging open questions in our
understanding of the function of neural networks. Comparing representations in
neural networks is fundamentally difficult as the structure of representations
varies greatly, even across groups of networks trained on identical tasks, and
over the course of training. Here, we develop projection weighted CCA
(Canonical Correlation Analysis) as a tool for understanding neural networks,
building off of SVCCA, a recently proposed method (Raghu et al., 2017). We
first improve the core method, showing how to differentiate between signal and
noise, and then apply this technique to compare across a group of CNNs,
demonstrating that networks which generalize converge to more similar
representations than networks which memorize, that wider networks converge to
more similar solutions than narrow networks, and that trained networks with
identical topology but different learning rates converge to distinct clusters
with diverse representations. We also investigate the representational dynamics
of RNNs, across both training and sequential timesteps, finding that RNNs
converge in a bottom-up pattern over the course of training and that the hidden
state is highly variable over the course of a sequence, even when accounting
for linear transforms. Together, these results provide new insights into the
function of CNNs and RNNs, and demonstrate the utility of using CCA to
understand representations.

papers.title: Uncovering Emergent Physics Representations Learned In-Context by Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do large language models implicitly learn physics during in-context learning, and do recognizable physical quantities emerge as distinct features in their internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that large language models can learn to forecast physical dynamics via in-context learning, and that energy-related features emerge in their residual stream activations, which are causally important for accurate predictions.
papers.conclusion: The results demonstrate that LLMs can internalize physical concepts like energy during in-context learning, suggesting transformer architectures can internalize abstract reasoning priors similar to human abstraction.
papers.key_findings:
Prediction accuracy for physical dynamics forecasting improves with longer context length.
Sparse activations from sparse autoencoders (SAEs) applied to residual streams correlate with energy quantities (total, kinetic, potential).
The correlation between sparse activations and energy is context-dependent and increases with longer contexts, especially for chaotic systems.
Intervention experiments ablating energy-correlated sparse activations degrade prediction accuracy, indicating their functional role.
Energy-related features are most prominently captured in the middle layers of the transformer.
papers.limitation: The study uses raw trajectory values as the sole input modality without external instructions or prompting strategies, leaving open whether chain-of-thought or structured prompts would strengthen correlations.
future_direction: Explore physics concepts beyond classical mechanics.
Investigate more human-aligned tasks such as answering conceptual questions from physics exams.
Leverage physics-informed tasks to understand internal mechanisms of large-scale models and advance LLM-based agents for physically realistic environments.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit impressive in-context learning (ICL) abilities, enabling them to solve wide range of tasks via textual prompts alone. As these capabilities advance, the range of applicable domains continues to expand significantly. However, identifying the precise mechanisms or internal structures within LLMs that allow successful ICL across diverse, distinct classes of tasks remains elusive. Physics-based tasks offer a promising testbed for probing this challenge. Unlike synthetic sequences such as basic arithmetic or symbolic equations, physical systems provide experimentally controllable, real-world data based on structured dynamics grounded in fundamental principles. This makes them particularly suitable for studying the emergent reasoning behaviors of LLMs in a realistic yet tractable setting. Here, we mechanistically investigate the ICL ability of LLMs, especially focusing on their ability to reason about physics. Using a dynamics forecasting task in physical systems as a proxy, we evaluate whether LLMs can learn physics in context. We first show that the performance of dynamics forecasting in context improves with longer input contexts. To uncover how such capability emerges in LLMs, we analyze the model's residual stream activations using sparse autoencoders (SAEs). Our experiments reveal that the features captured by SAEs correlate with key physical variables, such as energy. These findings demonstrate that meaningful physical concepts are encoded within LLMs during in-context learning. In sum, our work provides a novel case study that broadens our understanding of how LLMs learn in context.

papers.title: Causal-oriented representation learning for time-series forecasting based on the spatiotemporal information transformation
papers.research_question: How can causal analysis and multistep forecasting be jointly performed from a unified perspective to understand system dynamics?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Causal-oriented Representation Learning Predictor (CReP), a neural network framework that jointly conducts causal analysis and multistep forecasting from a unified perspective.
papers.conclusion: CReP effectively achieves multi-step-ahead forecasting and infers causal networks for target variables, offering a comprehensive understanding of system dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
CReP demonstrates satisfactory forecasting performance with low RMSE and high PCC on simulation models like Lorenz 96.
The framework successfully infers cause and effect networks for target variables, aligning with known causal structures.
CReP applies to real-world datasets, such as cardiovascular inpatients and COVID-19 spread, providing practical insights.
Ablation studies show that all loss components (reconstruction, future-consistency, orthogonal) are necessary for optimal performance.
The method is self-supervised and handles nonlinearity and non-separability better than Granger causality-based approaches.
papers.abstract: In real-world high-dimensional systems, both causal dependencies and temporal information of key variables are essential for dissecting the underlying mechanisms governing system dynamics. However, effective approaches to synthesize these two interconnected aspects for deeper insights remain lacking. Here we show a neural network framework, the Causal-oriented Representation Learning Predictor (CReP), which jointly conducts causal analysis and multistep forecasting from a unified perspective. CReP implicitly learns latent causal representations from observed data while simultaneously making multistep predictions, and explicitly interprets the representations to uncover the causes and effects of target variable. The core idea of CReP is to decompose the original space into three orthogonal latent factors, each capturing distinct causal representations: cause-related, effect-related, and non-causal representations of the target variable. The reconstruction-based dynamic causation, generalized through spatiotemporal information (STI) transformation mechanism, provides a theoretical foundation for simultaneously modeling causal interactions via latent representations and predicting future states using the effect representation. Evaluations on three simulation models and two real-world datasets demonstrate CReP’s robust forecasting accuracy and reliable causal insights. As a self-supervised-learning approach, CReP shows significant potential for practical applications and provides a unified framework to reveal intrinsic mechanisms in dynamical systems by integrating causal relationships and temporal information. In complex high-dimensional systems like power grids or COVID-19 transmission, both causal dependencies and temporal information of key variables are essential for dissecting the underlying mechanisms governing system dynamics. This paper presents Causal-oriented Representation Learning Predictor, a neural network framework designed to jointly conduct causal analysis and multistep forecasting.

papers.title: Decomposing Representation Space into Interpretable Subspaces with Unsupervised Learning
papers.research_question: Can we find interpretable subspaces in neural representations in an unsupervised way? To what extent are different aspects organized in separate subspaces?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an unsupervised method (NDM) to decompose representation space into interpretable subspaces, showing that these subspaces align with known circuit variables and can serve as new basic units for circuit analysis.
papers.conclusion: Unsupervised decomposition of representation space into interpretable subspaces is possible, and these subspaces can serve as new basic units for circuit analysis, offering a new perspective on understanding model internals.
papers.key_findings:
NDM can find interpretable subspaces without supervision, as shown in toy models and real language models.
Subspaces found by NDM align with variables in known circuits in GPT-2, as evidenced by high Gini coefficients in subspace patching experiments.
The method scales to 2B models, finding separate subspaces for context and parametric knowledge routing.
Qualitative analysis shows that subspaces are consistent and interpretable across different inputs.
papers.limitation: The method can get stuck in local minima, leading to sub-optimal subspace partitions.
future_direction: hierarchical structure of subspaces
more flexible searching over dimension configurations
applying the method to larger models and more tasks
papers.abstract: Understanding internal representations of neural models is a core interest of mechanistic interpretability. Due to its large dimensionality, the representation space can encode various aspects about inputs. To what extent are different aspects organized and encoded in separate subspaces? Is it possible to find these ``natural'' subspaces in a purely unsupervised way? Somewhat surprisingly, we can indeed achieve this and find interpretable subspaces by a seemingly unrelated training objective. Our method, neighbor distance minimization (NDM), learns non-basis-aligned subspaces in an unsupervised manner. Qualitative analysis shows subspaces are interpretable in many cases, and encoded information in obtained subspaces tends to share the same abstract concept across different inputs, making such subspaces similar to ``variables'' used by the model. We also conduct quantitative experiments using known circuits in GPT-2; results show a strong connection between subspaces and circuit variables. We also provide evidence showing scalability to 2B models by finding separate subspaces mediating context and parametric knowledge routing. Viewed more broadly, our findings offer a new perspective on understanding model internals and building circuits.

papers.title: The Non-Linear Representation Dilemma: Is Causal Abstraction Enough for Mechanistic Interpretability?
papers.research_question: Is causal abstraction sufficient for mechanistic interpretability when alignment maps are not constrained to be linear?
papers.core_contribution: Causal abstraction becomes vacuous when alignment maps are allowed to be arbitrarily complex, leading to the non-linear representation dilemma where there is no principled way to balance map complexity and accuracy.
papers.conclusion: Causal abstraction is not enough for mechanistic interpretability without assumptions about how models encode information.
papers.key_findings:
Theoretically, any algorithm can be perfectly mapped to any neural network under reasonable assumptions if alignment maps are arbitrarily complex.
Empirically, non-linear alignment maps can achieve near-perfect interchange intervention accuracy even on randomly initialized models that do not solve the task.
The complexity of alignment maps needed to achieve perfect IIA decreases as the model trains.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical result relies on assumptions such as input-injectivity and output-surjectivity of the neural network.
Empirical alignment map training can suffer from grokking and requires careful hyperparameter tuning.
future_direction: Studying the connection between information-encoding assumptions and causal abstraction.
papers.abstract: The concept of causal abstraction got recently popularised to demystify the opaque decision-making processes of machine learning models; in short, a neural network can be abstracted as a higher-level algorithm if there exists a function which allows us to map between them. Notably, most interpretability papers implement these maps as linear functions, motivated by the linear representation hypothesis: the idea that features are encoded linearly in a model's representations. However, this linearity constraint is not required by the definition of causal abstraction. In this work, we critically examine the concept of causal abstraction by considering arbitrarily powerful alignment maps. In particular, we prove that under reasonable assumptions, any neural network can be mapped to any algorithm, rendering this unrestricted notion of causal abstraction trivial and uninformative. We complement these theoretical findings with empirical evidence, demonstrating that it is possible to perfectly map models to algorithms even when these models are incapable of solving the actual task; e.g., on an experiment using randomly initialised language models, our alignment maps reach 100\% interchange-intervention accuracy on the indirect object identification task. This raises the non-linear representation dilemma: if we lift the linearity constraint imposed to alignment maps in causal abstraction analyses, we are left with no principled way to balance the inherent trade-off between these maps' complexity and accuracy. Together, these results suggest an answer to our title's question: causal abstraction is not enough for mechanistic interpretability, as it becomes vacuous without assumptions about how models encode information. Studying the connection between this information-encoding assumption and causal abstraction should lead to exciting future work.

papers.title: Disentangling Direction and Magnitude in Transformer Representations: A Double Dissociation Through L2-Matched Perturbation Analysis
papers.research_question: What are the distinct functional roles of direction (orientation) and magnitude (norm) in transformer hidden state representations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces L2-matched perturbation analysis to discover a double dissociation: angular perturbations disproportionately damage language modeling loss, while magnitude perturbations disproportionately damage syntactic accuracy, with distinct mechanistic pathways through attention and LayerNorm.
papers.conclusion: Direction and magnitude serve partially distinct computational roles in LayerNorm-based transformers: direction preferentially governs attentional routing, while magnitude encodes structural position and modulates processing intensity through LayerNorm.
papers.key_findings:
Angular perturbations cause up to 42.9× more damage to language modeling loss than magnitude perturbations at equal Euclidean displacement.
Magnitude perturbations cause up to 20.4% greater drop in syntactic accuracy (subject-verb agreement) than angular perturbations.
Causal intervention shows angular damage is substantially mediated by attention pathways (28.4% recovery via repair), while magnitude damage is substantially mediated by LayerNorm pathways (29.9% recovery).
The dissociation pattern replicates across scales within the Pythia architecture family but reverses in RMSNorm-based architectures like TinyLlama.
Magnitude correlates with parse tree depth, and disrupting this correlation explains why magnitude perturbations specifically impair syntactic processing.
papers.limitation:
L2 matching assumes equal Euclidean distance makes perturbations comparable, but neural networks operate in anisotropic spaces; angular perturbations amplify 3× more than magnitude by the final layer.
Angular perturbations use random orthogonal directions; results might differ for systematic rotations toward known feature directions.
Findings are specific to the Pythia/OPT architecture family and do not generalize to all transformers; the pattern reverses in RMSNorm-based architectures (TinyLlama).
Only middle layers (8–15) were targeted for intervention; early and late layers may show different patterns.
Syntactic evaluation is limited to subject-verb agreement from BLiMP; other syntactic phenomena may show different patterns.
Causal repair experiments account for only ~30% of each perturbation's damage; the remaining ~70% likely flows through MLP layers and residual connections.
future_direction: Feature-specific rotations (systematic rotations toward/away from known feature directions).
Investigating how the roles of direction and magnitude evolve during training.
Exploring magnitude as a confidence signal for uncertainty quantification.
Extending the methodology to other modalities (e.g., vision transformers).
Systematic comparison across normalization schemes (LayerNorm vs. RMSNorm).
papers.abstract: Transformer hidden states encode information as high-dimensional vectors, yet whether direction (orientation in representational space) and magnitude (vector norm) serve distinct functional roles remains unclear. Studying Pythia-family models, we discover a striking cross-over dissociation: angular perturbations cause up to 42.9 more damage to language modeling loss, while magnitude perturbations cause disproportionately more damage to syntactic processing (20.4% vs.1.6% accuracy drop on subject-verb agreement).This finding is enabled by L2-matched perturbation analysis, a methodology ensuring that an gular and magnitude perturbations achieve identical Euclidean displacements. Causal intervention reveals that angular damage flows substantially through the attention pathways (28.4% loss recovery via attention repair), while magnitude damage flows partly through the LayerNorm pathways(29.9% recovery via LayerNorm repair). These patterns replicate across scales within the Pythia architecture family. These findings provide evidence that direction and magnitude support partially distinct computational roles in LayerNorm based architectures. The direction preferentially affects attentional routing, while magnitude modulates processing intensity for fine-grained syntactic judgments. We find different patterns in RMSNorm-based architectures, suggesting that the dissociation depends on architectural choices. Our results refine the linear representation hypothesis and have implications for model editing and interpretability research

papers.title: Color Encoding in Latent Space of Stable Diffusion Models
papers.research_question: How is color information encoded in the latent space of Stable Diffusion models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that color in Stable Diffusion is encoded in opponent axes in latent channels c3 and c4, with intensity and shape in c1 and c2, showing an interpretable structure aligned with efficient coding.
papers.conclusion: The analysis shows that Stable Diffusion's latent space has a partially disentangled representation for color and shape, with specific channels dedicated to intensity, chromaticity, and spatial information, providing insights for model understanding and editing.
papers.key_findings:
Color presents an opponent representation based on Black-White, Cyan-Magenta, and Orange-Blue channels.
Chromatic information is mostly in channel 3 (Cyan-Magenta) and channel 4 (Orange-Blue), with channel 4 entangled with shape.
Shape is primarily encoded in channel 1 (Black-White), with some shape in channels 2 and 4.
Channel 2 encodes low-frequency shape information.
The latent space exhibits a partially disentangled representation for color and shape.
papers.limitation: Limitations in achieving fully disentangled representations using standard training procedures.
future_direction: Further research to condition generation based on latent channel manipulations.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in diffusion-based generative models have achieved remarkable visual fidelity, yet a detailed understanding of how specific perceptual attributes—such as color and shape—are internally represented remains limited. This work explores how color is encoded in a generative model through a systematic analysis of the latent representations in Stable Diffusion. Through controlled synthetic datasets, principal component analysis (PCA) and similarity metrics, we reveal that color information is encoded along circular, opponent axes predominantly captured in latent channels ⃗c3 and ⃗c4, whereas intensity and shape are primarily represented in channels ⃗c1 and ⃗c2. Our findings indicate that the latent space of Stable Diffusion exhibits an interpretable structure aligned with a efficient coding representation. These insights provide a foundation for future work in model understanding, editing applications, and the design of more disentangled generative frameworks.

papers.title: The Spotlight Resonance Method: Resolving the Alignment of Embedded Activations
papers.research_question: What causes the observed tendency of neural network representations to align with neurons (or a privileged basis)? The paper investigates whether this alignment is due to functional form choices, such as activation functions, that break symmetry and induce a privileged basis.
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces the Spotlight-Resonance Method (SRM), a versatile visualization tool for determining the axis alignment of embedded activations in deep learning models. It demonstrates that representations tend to align with a 'privileged basis' induced by functional form choices like activation functions, not due to any innate property of the standard neuron basis.
papers.conclusion: The Spotlight-Resonance Method is a simple, interpretable, and versatile tool for establishing representational alignment in deep learning models. It shows that alignment is caused by functional form choices (like activation functions) that induce a privileged basis, explaining prior observations.
papers.key_findings:
The Spotlight-Resonance Method (SRM) can detect whether embedded activations cluster around vectors of a privileged basis.
Representations in trained models tend to align (or anti-align) with the privileged basis vectors induced by the activation function.
The observed alignment with the standard basis in prior works is a consequence of elementwise activation functions privileging that basis, not a fundamental phenomenon.
The method can identify 'grandmother neurons' (neurons responding to specific human-interpretable concepts) in various networks.
The privileged basis is the fundamental quantity for representational alignment, not the standard basis.
future_direction: Expanding analysis on the functional form hierarchy of basis privileging.
More thoroughly investigating local coding through meaningful subsets of the dataset.
Exploring isotropic deep learning (including isotropic activation functions).
papers.abstract: Understanding how deep learning models represent data is currently difficult due to the limited number of methodologies available. This paper demonstrates a versatile and novel visualisation tool for determining the axis alignment of embedded data at any layer in any deep learning model. In particular, it evaluates the distribution around planes defined by the network's privileged basis vectors. This method provides both an atomistic and a holistic, intuitive metric for interpreting the distribution of activations across all planes. It ensures that both positive and negative signals contribute, treating the activation vector as a whole. Depending on the application, several variations of this technique are presented, with a resolution scale hyperparameter to probe different angular scales. Using this method, multiple examples are provided that demonstrate embedded representations tend to be axis-aligned with the privileged basis. This is not necessarily the standard basis, and it is found that activation functions directly result in privileged bases. Hence, it provides a direct causal link between functional form symmetry breaking and representational alignment, explaining why representations have a tendency to align with the neuron basis. Therefore, using this method, we begin to answer the fundamental question of what causes the observed tendency of representations to align with neurons. Finally, examples of so-called grandmother neurons are found in a variety of networks.

papers.title: Desiderata for Representation Learning: A Causal Perspective
papers.research_question: How can representation learning desiderata (non-spuriousness, efficiency, disentanglement) be formalized using causal notions, and how can metrics and algorithms be developed to learn such representations from single observational datasets?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a causal framework for representation learning that formalizes desiderata like non-spuriousness, efficiency, and disentanglement using counterfactual notions (probabilities of causation) and provides metrics and algorithms (CAUSAL-REP and IOSS) to learn such representations from single observational datasets.
papers.conclusion: Causality provides a fruitful perspective for representation learning, allowing intuitive desiderata to be formalized and leading to metrics and algorithms that can learn non-spurious and disentangled representations from single observational datasets.
papers.key_findings:
Non-spuriousness and efficiency in supervised representation learning can be formalized using probabilities of sufficiency (PS) and necessity (PN), leading to the CAUSAL-REP algorithm.
Disentanglement in unsupervised representation learning can be formalized via causal disentanglement, leading to the Independence-of-Support Score (IOSS) metric.
CAUSAL-REP learns non-spurious representations that improve out-of-distribution prediction on image and text datasets compared to baseline methods.
IOSS can distinguish disentangled from entangled representations better than existing unsupervised metrics on synthetic and real datasets.
The causal perspective enables the development of calculable metrics and algorithms for representation learning desiderata without requiring multiple environments or labeled features.
papers.limitation:
CAUSAL-REP requires the pinpointability condition (i.e., the unobserved common cause C can be pinpointed from X) for identification.
IOSS assumes compact support of the representation and may not apply to representations with unbounded support.
papers.abstract: Representation learning constructs low-dimensional representations to summarize essential features of high-dimensional data. This learning problem is often approached by describing various desiderata associated with learned representations; e.g., that they be non-spurious, efficient, or disentangled. It can be challenging, however, to turn these intuitive desiderata into formal criteria that can be measured and enhanced based on observed data. In this paper, we take a causal perspective on representation learning, formalizing non-spuriousness and efficiency (in supervised representation learning) and disentanglement (in unsupervised representation learning) using counterfactual quantities and observable consequences of causal assertions. This yields computable metrics that can be used to assess the degree to which representations satisfy the desiderata of interest and learn non-spurious and disentangled representations from single observational datasets.

papers.title: Do Llamas understand the periodic table?
papers.research_question: How do Large Language Models (LLMs) represent the periodic table of elements, and what is the geometric structure of their hidden states?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs internally develop structured geometric representations (a 3D spiral) of the periodic table in their hidden states, with knowledge encoded as continuous manifolds in middle layers that sharpen into categorical distinctions in deeper layers.
papers.conclusion: LLMs represent symbolic scientific knowledge as coherent, geometry-aware manifolds that reflect the natural order of the physical world, which can inform interpretability and trust in LLMs for scientific applications.
papers.key_findings:
A 3D spiral structure in LLM hidden states aligns with the conceptual organization of the periodic table.
Middle layers encode continuous, overlapping attribute subspaces, while deeper layers sharpen decision boundaries and integrate linguistic context.
Linguistic structure increasingly shapes factual representations in later layers.
Strong linear associations between related attributes in middle layers enable indirect recall.
Regression probing shows continuous numerical features are effectively represented in intermediate layers, while classification probing shows later layers are better for fine-grained categorical decisions.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to chemical elements in the periodic table; future studies could expand to other chemical structures and properties.
The hypothesis-driven validation of geometric structures may oversimplify LLMs' non-linear interactions.
future_direction: Expand to other chemical structures and properties.
Further investigation into how LLMs represent and reason about scientific knowledge.
papers.abstract: We observe a 3D spiral structure in the hidden states of LLMs that aligns with the conceptual structure of the periodic table.

papers.title: Reconstruction of Hidden Representation for Robust Feature Extraction
papers.research_question: How can we develop a robust approach to feature representation by analyzing properties of Auto-Encoder based algorithms and using corruption and reconstruction on both input and hidden representation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes Double Denoising Auto-Encoders (DDAEs), a new model that uses corruption and reconstruction on both input and hidden representation to learn invariant and robust feature representations, supported by theoretical analysis on the lower bound of reconstruction error and the robustness of hidden representation reconstruction.
papers.conclusion: DDAEs are an effective model for unsupervised representation learning, demonstrating superior performance over existing state-of-the-art models on multiple datasets by leveraging corruption and reconstruction on both input and hidden representation.
papers.key_findings:
The reconstruction error of the input in Auto-Encoder based algorithms has a lower bound, providing a guiding principle for reconstruction.
The necessary condition for the reconstruction of the input to reach the ideal state is that the reconstruction of hidden representation achieves its ideal condition.
Minimizing the Frobenius norm of the Jacobian matrix of the hidden representation has a deficiency and may lead to worse local optima, while minimizing the reconstruction error of the hidden representation is more robust.
DDAEs outperform Denoising Auto-Encoders (DAEs) and Contractive Auto-Encoders (CAEs) in learning robust feature representations, especially in the presence of noise or inessential features.
DDAEs can be trained with two different pre-training strategies (combined or separate optimization of the objective function) and achieve state-of-the-art performance on various datasets.
future_direction: Designing useful constraints or other operations on the hidden representation to develop more efficient representation learning models.
papers.abstract: This article aims to develop a new and robust approach to feature representation. Motivated by the success of Auto-Encoders, we first theoretically analyze and summarize the general properties of all algorithms that are based on traditional Auto-Encoders: (1) The reconstruction error of the input cannot be lower than a lower bound, which can be viewed as a guiding principle for reconstructing the input. Additionally, when the input is corrupted with noises, the reconstruction error of the corrupted input also cannot be lower than a lower bound. (2) The reconstruction of a hidden representation achieving its ideal situation is the necessary condition for the reconstruction of the input to reach the ideal state. (3) Minimizing the Frobenius norm of the Jacobian matrix of the hidden representation has a deficiency and may result in a much worse local optimum value. We believe that minimizing the reconstruction error of the hidden representation is more robust than minimizing the Frobenius norm of the Jacobian matrix of the hidden representation. Based on the above analysis, we propose a new model termed Double Denoising Auto-Encoders (DDAEs), which uses corruption and reconstruction on both the input and the hidden representation. We demonstrate that the proposed model is highly flexible and extensible and has a potentially better capability to learn invariant and robust feature representations. We also show that our model is more robust than Denoising Auto-Encoders (DAEs) for dealing with noises or inessential features. Furthermore, we detail how to train DDAEs with two different pretraining methods by optimizing the objective function in a combined and separate manner, respectively. Comparative experiments illustrate that the proposed model is significantly better for representation learning than the state-of-the-art models.

papers.title: Auto-Encoding Total Correlation Explanation
papers.research_question: How can we characterize disentanglement and dependence in representation learning using total correlation, and how does this relate to variational autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides an information-theoretic view of VAEs, showing the CorEx objective is equivalent to the VAE ELBO under certain conditions, and introduces AnchorVAE to make latent codes more interpretable through information maximization.
papers.conclusion: The information-theoretic perspective on unsupervised learning provides useful insights into the trade-off between information maximization and disentanglement, and leads to new methods for learning interpretable representations.
papers.key_findings:
The CorEx objective is equivalent to the VAE evidence lower bound (ELBO) under standard assumptions, providing a dual information-theoretic perspective.
Hierarchical VAEs (or stacking CorEx) lead to progressively more disentangled representations in higher layers.
AnchorVAE, which reweights the KL-divergence term for specific latent codes, can learn more interpretable latent factors by maximizing mutual information.
Sampling latent codes from the encoding distribution ∏ᵢ p(zᵢ) instead of a standard normal prior generates richer and more realistic images in VAEs.
papers.abstract: Advances in unsupervised learning enable reconstruction and generation of samples from complex distributions, but this success is marred by the inscrutability of the representations learned. We propose an information-theoretic approach to characterizing disentanglement and dependence in representation learning using multivariate mutual information, also called total correlation. The principle of total Cor-relation Ex-planation (CorEx) has motivated successful unsupervised learning applications across a variety of domains, but under some restrictive assumptions. Here we relax those restrictions by introducing a flexible variational lower bound to CorEx. Surprisingly, we find that this lower bound is equivalent to the one in variational autoencoders (VAE) under certain conditions. This information-theoretic view of VAE deepens our understanding of hierarchical VAE and motivates a new algorithm, AnchorVAE, that makes latent codes more interpretable through information maximization and enables generation of richer and more realistic samples.

papers.title: Decoding Diffusion: A Scalable Framework for Unsupervised Analysis of Latent Space Biases and Representations Using Natural Language Prompts
papers.research_question: How to automatically map latent directions in diffusion models to semantic concepts using natural language prompts for scalable analysis of biases and representations?
papers.core_contribution: A framework for unsupervised exploration of diffusion model latent spaces by mapping latent directions to natural language prompts, enabling automatic interpretation and broad concept analysis.
papers.conclusion: The method provides a scalable and versatile tool for interpreting diffusion model latent spaces, contributing to more transparent, interpretable, and ethically responsible generative models.
papers.key_findings:
The framework identifies gender biases in diffusion models, with professions like pilot and construction worker showing stronger male stereotypes.
Cosine distance between gendered and gender-neutral prompts correlates with the likelihood of generating female-presenting images.
Clustering of h-space vectors from food captions reveals semantic groups like square dishes and pots with soup.
The method enables automatic interpretation of latent directions without manual inspection.
It supports a broader range of analysis compared to previous methods limited by manual interpretation or few trained vectors.
papers.limitation: Variability due to random seed initialization affects the sampled h-space vectors.
future_direction: Reducing the effect of random seed initialization on sampled results
Extending analysis with quantifiable metrics on broader domains
papers.abstract: Recent advances in image generation have made diffusion models powerful tools for creating high-quality images. However, their iterative denoising process makes understanding and interpreting their semantic latent spaces more challenging than other generative models, such as GANs. Recent methods have attempted to address this issue by identifying semantically meaningful directions within the latent space. However, they often need manual interpretation or are limited in the number of vectors that can be trained, restricting their scope and utility. This paper proposes a novel framework for unsupervised exploration of diffusion latent spaces. We directly leverage natural language prompts and image captions to map latent directions. This method allows for the automatic understanding of hidden features and supports a broader range of analysis without the need to train specific vectors. Our method provides a more scalable and interpretable understanding of the semantic knowledge encoded within diffusion models, facilitating comprehensive analysis of latent biases and the nuanced representations these models learn. Experimental results show that our framework can uncover hidden patterns and associations in various domains, offering new insights into the interpretability of diffusion model latent spaces.

papers.title: A mathematical theory for understanding when abstract representations emerge in neural networks
papers.research_question: Under what conditions do abstract representations emerge in neural networks? Specifically, the paper investigates whether abstract representations are guaranteed to appear in feedforward networks trained on tasks that depend directly on latent variables.
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a mathematical theory proving that abstract representations are guaranteed to emerge in the hidden layer of feedforward nonlinear networks when trained on tasks that depend directly on latent variables, and develops a mean-field optimization framework to analyze such representations.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that abstract representations emerge naturally in neural networks trained on tasks with latent variables, providing a mathematical explanation for similar observations in neuroscience and machine learning, and offers a general framework for understanding representation geometry in task-optimized networks.
papers.key_findings:
For whitened and target-aligned inputs, ReLU networks develop abstract representations with parallelism score (PS) equal to 1 at global minima.
The optimal representation kernel takes the form K = a*11^T + b*K_Y, where K_Y is the output kernel.
The emergence of abstract representations is robust to the choice of activation function, holding for two broad classes of nonlinearities: threshold functions and odd functions.
The theory extends to multi-element classes (n ≥ 2) and deep feedforward architectures.
The framework provides a mean-field description where the optimal preactivation distribution satisfies a self-consistent condition.
papers.limitation:
The theory is limited to feedforward networks trained on tasks with binary latent variables and assumes the network reaches a global minimum.
The analysis assumes specific input geometries (whitened or target-aligned inputs) and may not cover all possible input structures.
future_direction: Extend the framework to other architectures such as ResNet and transformer models.
Analyze learning dynamics in networks trained with biological learning rules.
Investigate the Platonic representation hypothesis using the developed mathematical toolkit.
papers.abstract: Recent experiments reveal that task-relevant variables are often encoded in approximately orthogonal subspaces of the neural activity space. These disentangled low-dimensional representations are observed in multiple brain areas and across different species, and are typically the result of a process of abstraction that supports simple forms of out-of-distribution generalization. The mechanisms by which such geometries emerge remain poorly understood, and the mechanisms that have been investigated are typically unsupervised (e.g., based on variational auto-encoders). Here, we show mathematically that abstract representations of latent variables are guaranteed to appear in the last hidden layer of feedforward nonlinear networks when they are trained on tasks that depend directly on these latent variables. These abstract representations reflect the structure of the desired outputs or the semantics of the input stimuli. To investigate the neural representations that emerge in these networks, we develop an analytical framework that maps the optimization over the network weights into a mean-field problem over the distribution of neural preactivations. Applying this framework to a finite-width ReLU network, we find that its hidden layer exhibits an abstract representation at all global minima of the task objective. We further extend these analyses to two broad families of activation functions and deep feedforward architectures, demonstrating that abstract representations naturally arise in all these scenarios. Together, these results provide an explanation for the widely observed abstract representations in both the brain and artificial neural networks, as well as a mathematically tractable toolkit for understanding the emergence of different kinds of representations in task-optimized, feature-learning network models.

papers.title: The Origins of Representation Manifolds in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How are features represented as manifolds in large language models, and how does cosine similarity in representation space relate to the intrinsic geometry of features?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a mathematical framework to explain representation manifolds in LLMs, showing that under the continuous correspondence hypothesis, cosine similarity encodes the intrinsic geometry of features through shortest paths on the manifold, and validates this on text embeddings and token activations.
papers.conclusion: This work provides a formal mathematical framework to explain and interpret representation manifolds in large language models, validating the theory on internal representations and text embeddings, and revealing unexpected encodings of distances.
papers.key_findings:
Representation manifolds in LLMs reflect the topology of features (e.g., colors and dates form loops, years form a curve) as predicted by the continuous correspondence hypothesis.
Cosine similarity between feature representations locally reflects distance in the feature metric space, implying isometry up to scaling.
Years in GPT2-small are encoded on a logarithmic scale rather than linear, with larger distances between more recent years.
For colors in text-embedding-large-3, the representations follow a hue cycle rather than other possible encodings like RGB.
The manifold geometry allows linear computation of functions of the feature value, supporting the superposition hypothesis.
papers.limitation:
The hypothesis-driven approach is manual and not scalable, relying on a reasonable starting hypothesis for the metric space.
PCA may not capture the full complexity of distances encoded by the language model, which might be more complex and not correspond to human understanding.
Estimating manifolds in the presence of noise is statistically difficult, and the K-nearest-neighbour graph approach is prone to short-circuits causing errors.
future_direction: Learning the metric automatically rather than manual hypothesis
Developing 'manifold-aware' sparse autoencoders
Using the metric space formalism in future scientific discourse
papers.abstract: There is a large ongoing scientific effort in mechanistic interpretability to map embeddings and internal representations of AI systems into human-understandable concepts. A key element of this effort is the linear representation hypothesis, which posits that neural representations are sparse linear combinations of `almost-orthogonal' direction vectors, reflecting the presence or absence of different features. This model underpins the use of sparse autoencoders to recover features from representations. Moving towards a fuller model of features, in which neural representations could encode not just the presence but also a potentially continuous and multidimensional value for a feature, has been a subject of intense recent discourse. We describe why and how a feature might be represented as a manifold, demonstrating in particular that cosine similarity in representation space may encode the intrinsic geometry of a feature through shortest, on-manifold paths, potentially answering the question of how distance in representation space and relatedness in concept space could be connected. The critical assumptions and predictions of the theory are validated on text embeddings and token activations of large language models.

papers.title: Relative Geometry of Neural Forecasters: Linking Accuracy and Alignment in Learned Latent Geometry
papers.research_question: How do neural forecasters internally represent dynamical systems, and does the alignment of their latent geometries across model families correlate with forecasting accuracy?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces anchor-based relative embeddings to compare latent spaces of neural forecasters, revealing family-level alignment patterns and showing that alignment generally correlates with forecasting accuracy but high accuracy can coexist with low alignment (especially in transformers and ESNs).
papers.conclusion: Relative geometry provides a reproducible foundation for comparing how model families internalize dynamical structure, and alignment offers insights beyond task loss.
papers.key_findings:
Anchor-based relative embeddings remove rotational and scaling ambiguities, enabling direct comparison of latent spaces across model families.
MLPs align with other MLPs, RNNs with RNNs, while transformers and ESNs achieve strong forecasts despite weaker alignment.
Alignment generally correlates with forecasting accuracy, but high accuracy can coexist with low alignment (especially in transformers and ESNs).
The alignment signal stabilizes with increasing number of anchors (K>=16).
Noise and input length affect representational stability differently across forecasters.
papers.limitation: Alignment with the 'true system' refers only to alignment with the relative representation of observed trajectories, not to recovery of governing equations or physical state variables.
future_direction: Developing bridging mappings between model families
Alignment-driven training interventions
papers.abstract: Neural networks can accurately forecast complex dynamical systems, yet how they internally represent underlying latent geometry remains poorly understood. We study neural forecasters through the lens of representational alignment, introducing anchor-based, geometry-agnostic relative embeddings that remove rotational and scaling ambiguities in latent spaces. Applying this framework across seven canonical dynamical systems - ranging from periodic to chaotic - we reveal reproducible family-level structure: multilayer perceptrons align with other MLPs, recurrent networks with RNNs, while transformers and echo-state networks achieve strong forecasts despite weaker alignment. Alignment generally correlates with forecasting accuracy, yet high accuracy can coexist with low alignment. Relative geometry thus provides a simple, reproducible foundation for comparing how model families internalize and represent dynamical structure.

papers.title: Prediction of gene expression time series and structural analysis of gene regulatory networks using recurrent neural networks
