papers.research_question: How can we interpret deep neural networks and extract the features they learn from input data using maximum entropy methods?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a maximum entropy method for interpreting deep neural networks by sampling sequences that preserve penultimate layer activations, allowing extraction of learned features such as motifs and nucleosome positioning signals.
papers.conclusion: The maximum entropy method provides a valuable tool for interpreting deep neural networks, particularly in biological sequence analysis, and demonstrates synergy between statistical physics and machine learning for extracting subtle sequence features.
papers.key_findings:
The MaxEnt method successfully captures XOR logic learned by a simple ANN, while Saliency Map and DeepLIFT methods fail to do so.
The MaxEnt method localizes CTCF binding motifs with better agreement with conventional motif discovery tools (MEME/FIMO) than Saliency Map and DeepLIFT.
The MaxEnt method extracts nucleosome positioning signals, including periodic GC content at 10 bp intervals, more effectively than Saliency Map and DeepLIFT.
The method can assess the importance of global sequence features (e.g., GC content) via a feature importance score derived from the variance of MCMC samples.
Features extracted by MaxEnt (low-variance principal components) can be used for classification, as demonstrated by a nearest neighbor classifier achieving 76% accuracy.
papers.limitation: The MaxEnt method is computationally expensive compared to Saliency Map and DeepLIFT due to MCMC sampling.
papers.abstract: New architectures of multilayer artificial neural networks and new methods for training them are rapidly revolutionizing the application of machine learning in diverse fields, including business, social science, physical sciences, and biology. Interpreting deep neural networks, however, currently remains elusive, and a critical challenge lies in understanding which meaningful features a network is actually learning. We present a general method for interpreting deep neural networks and extracting network-learned features from input data. We describe our algorithm in the context of biological sequence analysis. Our approach, based on ideas from statistical physics, samples from the maximum entropy distribution over possible sequences, anchored at an input sequence and subject to constraints implied by the empirical function learned by a network. Using our framework, we demonstrate that local transcription factor binding motifs can be identified from a network trained on ChIP-seq data and that nucleosome positioning signals are indeed learned by a network trained on chemical cleavage nucleosome maps. Imposing a further constraint on the maximum entropy distribution also allows us to probe whether a network is learning global sequence features, such as the high GC content in nucleosome-rich regions. This work thus provides valuable mathematical tools for interpreting and extracting learned features from feed-forward neural networks.

papers.title: Insights on representational similarity in neural networks with canonical correlation
papers.research_question: How can we compare neural network representations and understand their evolution over time? The paper develops projection weighted CCA to address this.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces projection weighted CCA, an improved method for comparing neural network representations, and uses it to show that generalizing networks converge to more similar representations than memorizing networks, wider networks converge to more similar solutions, and RNNs exhibit bottom-up convergence during training.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that projection weighted CCA is a useful tool for analyzing neural network representations, revealing insights about convergence and similarity across networks and over time.
papers.key_findings:
Networks that generalize converge to more similar representations than those that memorize.
Wider networks converge to more similar solutions than narrower networks.
Networks with identical topology but different learning rates converge to distinct clusters of solutions.
RNNs exhibit bottom-up convergence over the course of training.
RNN hidden states vary nonlinearly across sequence timesteps, even when accounting for linear transforms.
future_direction: Examine what is unique about directions preserved across networks trained with different initializations.
Explore whether the insight about similarity and generalization could be used as a regularizer to improve network performance.
Investigate which aspects of RNN representations are stable over time and which vary.
papers.abstract: Comparing different neural network representations and determining how representations evolve over time remain challenging open questions in our understanding of the function of neural networks. Comparing representations in neural networks is fundamentally difficult as the structure of representations varies greatly, even across groups of networks trained on identical tasks, and over the course of training. Here, we develop projection weighted CCA (Canonical Correlation Analysis) as a tool for understanding neural networks, building off of SVCCA, a recently proposed method (Raghu et al., 2017). We first improve the core method, showing how to differentiate between signal and noise, and then apply this technique to compare across a group of CNNs, demonstrating that networks which generalize converge to more similar representations than networks which memorize, that wider networks converge to more similar solutions than narrow networks, and that trained networks with identical topology but different learning rates converge to distinct clusters with diverse representations. We also investigate the representational dynamics of RNNs, across both training and sequential timesteps, finding that RNNs converge in a bottom-up pattern over the course of training and that the hidden state is highly variable over the course of a sequence, even when accounting for linear transforms. Together, these results provide new insights into the function of CNNs and RNNs, and demonstrate the utility of using CCA to understand representations.

papers.title: Embryology of a Language Model
papers.research_question: How does a language model develop its internal computational structure over training, visualized through an embryological approach using susceptibilities and UMAP?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an embryological approach applying UMAP to susceptibility matrices to visualize the structural development of a language model over training, revealing a clear 'body plan' and discovering novel structures like the 'spacing fin'.
papers.conclusion: Susceptibility analysis combined with UMAP provides a powerful, holistic lens for studying the developmental principles of complex neural networks, enabling the discovery of novel computational structures.
papers.key_findings:
UMAP projections of susceptibility vectors reveal a 'rainbow serpent' structure stratified by token patterns, showing the model's internal organization.
The emergence of the induction circuit is visible as a thickening of the dorsal-ventral axis in the UMAP.
A previously unknown 'spacing fin' structure dedicated to counting space tokens is discovered and visualized.
The overall structure and its development are remarkably similar across different random seeds, suggesting a universal body plan.
The method demonstrates that susceptibility analysis can move beyond validation to uncover novel mechanisms.
papers.limitation:
UMAP does not preserve global structure and represents data as roughly uniformly dense even when that is not the case, introducing potential for error in dimensionality reduction.
Lack of a complete mechanistic explanation for how the spacing fin structure operates.
future_direction: Investigate whether qualitative changes in susceptibilities are associated with changes in the geometry of the loss landscape.
Target the spacing fin for more mechanistic analysis to understand its operation.
Connect the geometry of the UMAP representation to the learned representation within the model.
papers.abstract: Understanding how language models develop their internal computational structure is a central problem in the science of deep learning. While susceptibilities, drawn from statistical physics, offer a promising analytical tool, their full potential for visualizing network organization remains untapped. In this work, we introduce an embryological approach, applying UMAP to the susceptibility matrix to visualize the model's structural development over training. Our visualizations reveal the emergence of a clear ``body plan,'' charting the formation of known features like the induction circuit and discovering previously unknown structures, such as a ``spacing fin'' dedicated to counting space tokens. This work demonstrates that susceptibility analysis can move beyond validation to uncover novel mechanisms, providing a powerful, holistic lens for studying the developmental principles of complex neural networks.

papers.title: Hallmarks of Optimization Trajectories in Neural Networks: Directional Exploration and Redundancy
papers.research_question: How are optimization trajectories structured in neural networks, and how do they depend on hyperparameters and scale?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces trajectory maps and associated hallmarks to analyze the directional structure of optimization trajectories, revealing how hyperparameters affect directional exploration, how scale regularizes trajectories, and demonstrating redundancy that can be exploited for efficient training.
papers.conclusion: Trajectory maps provide a powerful tool for understanding optimization dynamics, revealing directional exploration and redundancy, and suggesting potential for hybrid optimization schemes.
papers.key_findings:
Optimization trajectories are highly structured, with high mean directional similarity, indicating directional redundancy.
Momentum and weight decay encourage directional exploration, leading to better solutions.
Scale regularizes trajectories, increasing cosine similarity between parameters across training.
There is heterogeneity in Q,K,V dynamics in middle attention layers of LLMs, which homogenizes with scale.
Directional redundancy allows training only batchnorm parameters after a certain point to match full network performance.
papers.limitation:
Our analysis is limited to the parameter space and does not consider the function space directly.
Experiments with training scalar parameters are based on vision models due to resource constraints for LLMs.
future_direction: Develop a version of MDS weighted by step lengths.
Exploit directional redundancy for more efficient training of LLMs.
papers.abstract: We propose a fresh take on understanding the mechanisms of neural networks by analyzing the rich directional structure of optimization trajectories, represented by their pointwise parameters. Towards this end, we introduce some natural notions of the complexity of optimization trajectories, both qualitative and quantitative, which hallmark the directional nature of optimization in neural networks: when is there redundancy, and when exploration. We use them to reveal the inherent nuance and interplay involved between various optimization choices, such as momentum and weight decay. Further, the trajectory perspective helps us see the effect of scale on regularizing the directional nature of trajectories, and as a by-product, we also observe an intriguing heterogeneity of Q,K,V dynamics in the middle attention layers in LLMs and which is homogenized by scale. Importantly, we put the significant directional redundancy observed to the test by demonstrating that training only scalar batchnorm parameters some while into training matches the performance of training the entire network, which thus exhibits the potential of hybrid optimization schemes that are geared towards efficiency.

papers.title: Eliciting Latent Knowledge from Quirky Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we elicit latent knowledge from language models that are finetuned to make systematic errors, using probes on their activations?
papers.core_contribution: Linear probes on middle-layer activations can extract context-independent knowledge from language models finetuned to output untruthfully, enabling elicitation of correct answers despite deceptive outputs.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that context-independent representations of knowledge exist in quirky models, and probing methods can reliably extract truth, informing scalable oversight of capable systems.
papers.key_findings:
Probes trained on truthful contexts generalize to untruthful contexts, indicating context-independent knowledge representations.
The best probing method (logistic regression on contrast pairs) recovers 75% of the performance gap between truthful and untruthful behavior on hard examples.
Mechanistic anomaly detection using Mahalanobis distance can flag untruthful behavior with an average AUROC of 0.95.
Difference-in-means probing directions are more causally implicated in model output and show better robustness to distribution shifts.
Unsupervised methods like CCS and CRC have an inductive bias towards context-independent generalization but achieve lower in-distribution performance.
papers.limitation:
Measurement of difficulty is a significant limitation, as different difficulty metrics are minimally correlated.
Contrast pair activations come from the answer token position, which is out-of-distribution for the finetuning data.
future_direction: Expand on the diversity and representativeness of evaluations by constructing new quirky datasets and models.
Investigate the limits of context-independent representations by varying the number of personas in finetuning.
Characterize the causal mechanisms involved, such as how intervening on knowledge representations affects output.
papers.abstract: Eliciting Latent Knowledge (ELK) aims to find patterns in a capable neural network's activations that robustly track the true state of the world, especially in hard-to-verify cases where the model's output is untrusted. To further ELK research, we introduce 12 datasets and a corresponding suite of "quirky" language models (LMs) that are finetuned to make systematic errors when answering questions if and only if the keyword "Bob" is present in the prompt. We find that, especially in middle layers, linear probes usually report an LM's knowledge independently of what the LM outputs, enabling us to elicit the correct answer despite the model's untruthful output. The best probing method (logistic regression on contrast pairs) recovers 89% of the gap in AUROC between truthful and untruthful contexts, and 75% for questions harder than those used to train the probe. We also find that a mechanistic anomaly detection approach can flag untruthful behavior with 0.95 AUROC. Our results show promise for eliciting reliable knowledge from capable but untrusted models, and facilitates future research empirically investigating ELK methods.

papers.title: Coding with transient trajectories in recurrent neural networks
papers.research_question: What are the dynamical mechanisms that enable transient amplification in recurrent neural networks, and how can networks be designed to implement specific transient trajectories for coding?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a criterion for transient amplification in linear recurrent networks based on the symmetric part of the connectivity matrix, and constructs minimal low-rank networks that implement specific input-output mappings via amplified transients.
papers.conclusion: Transient coding in recurrent networks is enabled by non-normal connectivity satisfying a simple criterion, and such networks can be engineered to robustly encode multiple stimuli through amplified trajectories.
papers.key_findings:
Transient amplification occurs if the largest eigenvalue of the symmetric part of the connectivity matrix JS is greater than 1.
In random Gaussian networks, amplification occurs when the connection strength g is between 1/√2 and 1.
Amplified inputs and their corresponding readouts are given by the right and left singular vectors of the propagator matrix.
Low-rank connectivity matrices can be designed to map specific input directions to output directions through two-dimensional transient trajectories.
The capacity of such networks, i.e., the number of orthogonal stimuli that can be encoded, scales linearly with network size.
papers.abstract: Following a stimulus, the neural response typically strongly varies in time and across neurons before settling to a steady-state. While classical population coding theory disregards the temporal dimension, recent works have argued that trajectories of transient activity can be particularly informative about stimulus identity and may form the basis of computations through dynamics. Yet the dynamical mechanisms needed to generate a population code based on transient trajectories have not been fully elucidated. Here we examine transient coding in a broad class of high-dimensional linear networks of recurrently connected units. We start by reviewing a well-known result that leads to a distinction between two classes of networks: networks in which all inputs lead to weak, decaying transients, and networks in which specific inputs elicit amplified transient responses and are mapped onto output states during the dynamics. Theses two classes are simply distinguished based on the spectrum of the symmetric part of the connectivity matrix. For the second class of networks, which is a sub-class of non-normal networks, we provide a procedure to identify transiently amplified inputs and the corresponding readouts. We first apply these results to standard randomly-connected and two-population networks. We then build minimal, low-rank networks that robustly implement trajectories mapping a specific input onto a specific orthogonal output state. Finally, we demonstrate that the capacity of the obtained networks increases proportionally with their size.

papers.title: On the Predictive Power of Representation Dispersion in Language Models
papers.research_question: How does the dispersion of hidden representations in language models correlate with perplexity, and can this be leveraged for practical applications like model selection and training?
papers.core_contribution: The paper establishes a strong negative correlation between representation dispersion (average pairwise cosine distance) and perplexity in language models, and demonstrates how this geometric property can be used for label-free performance prediction, model selection, layer selection for retrieval augmentation, and as a training signal.
papers.conclusion: Representation dispersion serves as both a practical diagnostic and a training signal for language models, correlating with downstream performance and enabling efficient model selection, layer selection for kNN-LM, and improved training.
papers.key_findings:
Representation dispersion strongly and negatively correlates with perplexity across diverse model families and text domains.
Dispersion measured on unlabeled text can predict downstream accuracy, enabling data-efficient model selection and slice discovery.
The dispersion gap (combining within-domain and between-domain token distances) serves as a robust, label-free proxy for task performance in domains like math and code.
In kNN-LM, choosing the hidden layer with the highest dispersion yields the best perplexity, providing an unsupervised shortcut for sub-layer selection.
Incorporating a simple 'push-away' auxiliary loss during training increases dispersion and directly improves perplexity in both single-domain and cross-domain scenarios.
papers.limitation:
Focus on average pairwise cosine distance may not capture all nuanced aspects of embedding geometry or model behavior.
Causality between dispersion and performance cannot be definitively concluded; certain architectures or objectives may modulate this relationship.
Experiments are primarily on English text from standard benchmarks and a limited set of specialized domains; generalizability to other languages, modalities, or highly domain-specific corpora is unclear.
future_direction: Investigate how representation dispersion interacts with other design choices such as architectural variations or tokenization strategies.
Explore whether additional regularization signals might further strengthen model robustness and interpretability.
papers.abstract: We show that a language model's ability to predict text is tightly linked to the breadth of its embedding space: models that spread their contextual representations more widely tend to achieve lower perplexity. Concretely, we find that representation dispersion - the average pairwise cosine distance among hidden vectors - strongly and negatively correlates with perplexity across diverse model families (LLaMA, Qwen, and others) and domains (Wikipedia, news, scientific abstracts). Beyond illustrating this link, we show how dispersion can be leveraged for a range of practical tasks without requiring labeled data. First, measuring dispersion on unlabeled text allows us to predict downstream accuracy in new domains, offering a data-efficient tool for model selection. Next, we find that identifying layers with higher dispersion pinpoints the best representations for retrieval-based methods such as kNN-LM, bypassing exhaustive layer-by-layer searches. Finally, we integrate a simple push-away objective into training, which increases dispersion in both single-domain and cross-domain scenarios and directly improves perplexity in each.

papers.title: Towards Explainability of the Latent Space by Disentangled Representation Learning
papers.research_question: How to discover explainable directions in the latent space of generative models to achieve disentangled and interpretable representations?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a novel pipeline for explainable disentangled representation learning that combines a Dirichlet semantic autoencoder, conditional deterministic diffusion, group-swap, and latent traversal to disentangle and explain the latent space.
papers.conclusion: The proposed pipeline combining Dirichlet variational autoencoder, conditional diffusion, group-swap, and latent traversal can disentangle and explain the latent space, improving representation explainability.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed pipeline can disentangle and explain the latent space of generative models.
The Dirichlet variational autoencoder improves concept disentangling in the latent space.
Group-swapping and latent traversal are key to promoting representation explainability and understanding semantic information.
future_direction: Explore the practical implications of the pipeline in image processing.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks are widely used in computer vision for image classification, segmentation and generation. They are also often criticised as “black boxes” because their decision-making process is often not interpretable by humans. However, learning explainable representations that explicitly disentangle the underlying mechanisms that structure observational data is still a challenge. To further explore the latent space and achieve generic processing, we propose a pipeline for discovering the explainable directions in the latent space of generative models. Since the latent space contains semantically meaningful directions and can be explained, we propose a pipeline to fully resolve the representation of the latent space. It consists of a Dirichlet encoder, conditional deterministic diffusion, a group-swap and a latent traversal module. We believe that this study provides an insight into the advancement of research explaining the disentanglement of neural networks in the community.

papers.title: Partial Symmetry Enforced Attention Decomposition (PSEAD): A Group-Theoretic Framework for Equivariant Transformers in Biological Systems
papers.research_question: How can local, partial, and approximate symmetries inherent in biological data be embedded into Transformer self-attention to improve generalization, interpretability, and computational efficiency?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Partial Symmetry Enforced Attention Decomposition (PSEAD) framework, a group-theoretic method that decomposes Transformer self-attention into orthogonal irreducible components aligned with local symmetry subgroups, enabling models to learn and exploit partial symmetries in biological data.
papers.conclusion: PSEAD offers a principled paradigm for advancing machine learning in biology by embedding symmetry-aware inductive biases into Transformers, leading to more performant and insightful AI systems for understanding biological systems.
papers.key_findings:
The self-attention mechanism is inherently equivariant under local permutation group actions, allowing for a principled decomposition into symmetry-specific components.
PSEAD is expected to improve generalization to novel motifs with similar partial symmetries, enhance interpretability via symmetry-channel analysis, and increase computational efficiency by focusing on relevant symmetric subspaces.
The framework can be extended to dynamic biological processes in reinforcement learning, such as protein folding and drug discovery.
papers.limitation:
The framework currently focuses on finite permutation groups and requires specifying the target symmetry group a priori; it does not automatically learn or infer symmetries from data.
Real biological symmetries are often approximate due to noise, mutations, or conformational flexibility, and the framework's robustness to such approximations requires further research.
future_direction: Extension to continuous symmetry groups (e.g., SO(3), SE(3)) using harmonic analysis.
Development of multi-resolution equivariant models that integrate symmetries across different scales.
Adaptive symmetry detection to learn relevant local symmetry groups from data without prior specification.
Integration with causal inference to identify causal relationships via symmetry-disentangled features.
Enhanced robustness to approximate symmetries through soft projection or statistical modeling.
Optimized computational implementations for large-scale biological datasets.
papers.abstract: This research introduces the Theory of Partial Symmetry Enforced Attention Decomposition (PSEAD), a new and rigorous group-theoretic framework designed to seamlessly integrate local symmetry awareness into the core architecture of self-attention mechanisms within Transformer models. We formalize the concept of local permutation subgroup actions on windows of biological data, proving that under such actions, the attention mechanism naturally decomposes into a direct sum of orthogonal irreducible components. Critically, these components are intrinsically aligned with the irreducible representations of the acting permutation subgroup, thereby providing a powerful mathematical basis for disentangling symmetric and asymmetric features. We show that PSEAD offers substantial advantages. These include enhanced generalization capabilities to novel biological motifs exhibiting similar partial symmetries, unprecedented interpretability by allowing direct visualization and analysis of attention contributions from different symmetry channels, and significant computational efficiency gains by focusing representational capacity on relevant symmetric subspaces. Beyond static data analysis, we extend PSEAD's applicability to dynamic biological processes within reinforcement learning paradigms, showcasing its potential to accelerate the discovery and optimization of biologically meaningful policies in complex environments like protein folding and drug discovery. This work lays the groundwork for a new generation of biologically informed, symmetry-aware artificial intelligence models.

papers.title: Unsupervised learning in images and audio to produce neural receptive fields: a primer and accessible notebook
papers.research_question: How can unsupervised learning, specifically Independent Component Analysis (ICA), model early sensory processing in vision and audition, and how does it compare to Principal Component Analysis (PCA)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a consolidated review and demonstration of Independent Component Analysis (ICA) as an efficient neural coding scheme for early sensory processing, showing that ICA produces receptive field models similar to physiological ones for natural inputs, and provides an accessible Jupyter notebook for educational and research purposes.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that ICA is a neurally appropriate efficient coding strategy for natural sensory data, and the provided Jupyter notebook demonstrates the principle in an accessible way for educational and research purposes.
papers.key_findings:
ICA produces filters resembling biological receptive fields (Gabor-like for vision, gammatone-like for audition) when applied to natural inputs, while PCA does not.
Non-natural inputs do not yield neural-like filters with ICA, indicating that both the coding objective and the natural statistics of the input are necessary.
The same five-step computational strategy can model early sensory processing across modalities (grayscale, color, audio) with only a change in inputs.
papers.limitation:
The demonstration uses a relatively small dataset of images from the internet which can bias the results.
Evaluation is by visual comparison only, without empirical or statistical evaluation.
Only grayscale, color, and audio modalities are demonstrated; video and binocular modalities are not included.
future_direction: Include video and binocular modalities in the notebook.
Use larger datasets and empirical evaluation of derived filters.
Explore the use of ICA filters as pre-trained features in deep learning models.
papers.abstract: Abstract Sensory processing relies on efficient computation driven by a combination of low-level unsupervised, statistical structural learning, and high-level task-dependent learning. In the earliest stages of sensory processing, sparse and independent coding strategies are capable of modeling neural processing using the same coding strategy with only a change in the input (e.g., grayscale images, color images, and audio). We present a consolidated review of Independent Component Analysis (ICA) as an efficient neural coding scheme with the ability to model early visual and auditory neural processing. We created a self-contained, accessible Jupyter notebook using Python to demonstrate the efficient coding principle for different modalities following a consistent five-step strategy. For each modality, derived receptive field models from natural and non-natural inputs are contrasted, demonstrating how neural codes are not produced when the inputs sufficiently deviate from those animals were evolved to process. Additionally, the demonstration shows that ICA produces more neurally-appropriate receptive field models than those based on common compression strategies, such as Principal Component Analysis. The five-step strategy not only produces neural-like models but also promotes reuse of code to emphasize the input-agnostic nature where each modality can be modeled with only a change in inputs. This notebook can be used to readily observe the links between unsupervised machine learning strategies and early sensory neuroscience, improving our understanding of flexible data-driven neural development in nature and future applications.

papers.title: The Representation and Recall of Interwoven Structured Knowledge in LLMs: A Geometric and Layered Analysis
papers.research_question: How do LLMs encode interwoven scientific knowledge, and do they reflect geometric structures like the periodic table?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs encode scientific knowledge in geometric structures, such as a 3D spiral aligning with the periodic table, representing knowledge as interwoven manifolds rather than isolated facts.
papers.conclusion: LLMs develop internal representations that reflect the structured geometry of scientific knowledge, representing symbolic knowledge as geometry-aware, interwoven manifolds.
papers.key_findings:
A 3D spiral structure is observed in hidden states that aligns with the periodic table.
Middle layers encode continuous attributes enabling indirect recall, while deeper layers sharpen categorical distinctions.
Linguistic context increasingly shapes representations in later layers.
Middle layers have strong linear associations between related attributes, which weaken in deeper layers.
papers.limitation:
Prompts are focused on chemical elements and may not extend to domains with more abstract features.
Hypothesis-driven validation may oversimplify LLMs' non-linear interactions.
future_direction: Further investigation into how LLMs represent and reason about scientific knowledge, such as materials property prediction.
Informing the design of downstream embedding-based tasks.
papers.abstract: This study investigates how large language models (LLMs) represent and recall multi-associated attributes across transformer layers. We show that intermediate layers encode factual knowledge by superimposing related attributes in overlapping spaces, along with effective recall even when attributes are not explicitly prompted. In contrast, later layers refine linguistic patterns and progressively separate attribute representations, optimizing task-specific outputs while appropriately narrowing attribute recall. We identify diverse encoding patterns including, for the first time, the observation of 3D spiral structures when exploring information related to the periodic table of elements. Our findings reveal a dynamic transition in attribute representations across layers, contributing to mechanistic interpretability and providing insights for understanding how LLMs handle complex, interrelated knowledge.

papers.title: Beyond Geometry: Comparing the Temporal Structure of Computation in Neural Circuits with Dynamical Similarity Analysis
papers.research_question: How can we tell whether two neural networks utilize the same internal processes for a particular computation? The paper investigates this by comparing networks at the level of dynamics rather than geometry.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Dynamical Similarity Analysis (DSA), a method to compare neural networks based on their dynamics rather than geometry, enabling identification of equivalent computations despite geometric differences.
papers.conclusion: DSA provides a powerful tool for comparing neural networks at the level of dynamics, with applications in model validation, brain-computer interfaces, and understanding learning rules.
papers.key_findings:
DSA identifies dynamical similarities between RNNs despite differences in geometry (e.g., different architectures and activation functions).
DSA distinguishes systems with different dynamics (bistable, line attractor, point attractor) even when their condition-averaged trajectories are geometrically similar.
DSA is invariant under smooth geometric deformations that preserve attractor topology (e.g., ring attractor).
DSA responds to changes in topology (e.g., transforming a ring attractor into a line attractor).
DSA can disentangle different learning rules (e.g., Adam, SGD with Momentum, Feedback Alignment) in an unsupervised manner from training dynamics.
papers.limitation:
It can be challenging to identify the optimal DMD hyperparameters.
DSA requires that the data are sampled uniformly in time.
The method assumes that the dynamics can be approximated by a linear model in the embedding space.
future_direction: Apply DSA to experimental neural data.
Use DSA for rapid alignment of Brain-Computer Interfaces (BCI) across days.
papers.abstract: How can we tell whether two neural networks utilize the same internal processes for a particular computation? This question is pertinent for multiple subfields of neuroscience and machine learning, including neuroAI, mechanistic interpretability, and brain-machine interfaces. Standard approaches for comparing neural networks focus on the spatial geometry of latent states. Yet in recurrent networks, computations are implemented at the level of dynamics, and two networks performing the same computation with equivalent dynamics need not exhibit the same geometry. To bridge this gap, we introduce a novel similarity metric that compares two systems at the level of their dynamics, called Dynamical Similarity Analysis (DSA). Our method incorporates two components: Using recent advances in data-driven dynamical systems theory, we learn a high-dimensional linear system that accurately captures core features of the original nonlinear dynamics. Next, we compare different systems passed through this embedding using a novel extension of Procrustes Analysis that accounts for how vector fields change under orthogonal transformation. In four case studies, we demonstrate that our method disentangles conjugate and non-conjugate recurrent neural networks (RNNs), while geometric methods fall short. We additionally show that our method can distinguish learning rules in an unsupervised manner. Our method opens the door to comparative analyses of the essential temporal structure of computation in neural circuits.

papers.title: Feature Forgetting in Continual Representation Learning
papers.research_question: What are the characteristics of representation learning in continual learning, and how does feature forgetting affect it?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a protocol for evaluating representation in continual learning, identifies feature forgetting as a key deficiency, and proposes gating adapters to mitigate feature forgetting, thereby improving representation learning.
papers.conclusion: Representation learning and catastrophic forgetting are largely separate issues in continual learning, and improving representation learning benefits both old and new tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Representation learning in continual learning is consistently deficient compared to multi-task learning, and the gap increases with the number of tasks.
Feature forgetting is a prevalent problem in continual learning, where previously learned features are erased and have to be re-learned.
Common techniques for mitigating catastrophic forgetting (e.g., regularization, replay) have little effect on improving representation learning.
Gating adapters, which selectively activate units based on task features, can mitigate feature forgetting and improve representation learning.
Improving representation learning can also improve average accuracy on past tasks when combined with rehearsal methods.
papers.limitation:
The study investigates feature forgetting, which is only one of the limiting factors of representation learning; other factors like gradient noise and negative transfer are not addressed.
The study does not cover other representation modalities such as text or other models such as Transformers.
future_direction: Further investigation on the representation learning component of continual and lifelong learning.
Expanding the discussion to other representation modalities such as text and other models such as Transformers.
Studying the combination of adapters with conventional forgetting-mitigation methods such as replay.
papers.abstract: In continual and lifelong learning, good representation learning can help increase performance and reduce sample complexity when learning new tasks. There is evidence that representations do not suffer from "catastrophic forgetting" even in plain continual learning, but little further fact is known about its characteristics. In this paper, we aim to gain more understanding about representation learning in continual learning, especially on the feature forgetting problem. We devise a protocol for evaluating representation in continual learning, and then use it to present an overview of the basic trends of continual representation learning, showing its consistent deficiency and potential issues. To study the feature forgetting problem, we create a synthetic dataset to identify and visualize the prevalence of feature forgetting in neural networks. Finally, we propose a simple technique using gating adapters to mitigate feature forgetting. We conclude by discussing that improving representation learning benefits both old and new tasks in continual learning.

papers.title: Unsupervised learning on spontaneous retinal activity leads to efficient neural representation geometry
papers.research_question: Can pre-training on movies of retinal waves improve object recognition in neural networks, and how does it affect the geometry of internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: Pre-training neural networks on retinal waves improves performance on spatial translation tasks and leads to more linearly separable feature representations, as explained by manifold geometry.
papers.conclusion: Retinal waves can instruct the formation of visual representations that support object recognition, and their spatiotemporal properties prepare networks for higher-order feature extraction.
papers.key_findings:
Pre-training on retinal waves significantly improves performance on spatial translation tasks, while slightly improving image classification and color change tasks.
Networks pre-trained on retinal waves show increased separability (capacity) of object manifolds for spatial translation, with decreased manifold dimension and radius.
Pre-training reduces inter-manifold correlations and maintains an effective dimensionality of the feature space, avoiding vanishing or exploding dimensionality.
The spatiotemporal characteristics of retinal waves are necessary for learning spatial invariance; shuffling spatial or temporal structure reduces performance.
Real and simulated retinal waves yield similar results, suggesting common spatiotemporal features drive the effects.
papers.limitation:
Findings are subject to the choice of network architecture (ResNet-18), learning algorithm (SimCLR), and dataset (postnatal mouse retinal waves).
Retinal waves are not the only form of spontaneous activity during development.
future_direction: Consider the role of cortical feedback and introduce bioplausible, synaptically local learning rules.
Investigate the role of spontaneous activity in other modalities like temporal prediction.
Perform laboratory experiments in mice to verify model predictions and study neural object manifolds at the onset of vision.
papers.abstract: Prior to the onset of vision, neurons in the developing mammalian retina spontaneously fire in correlated activity patterns known as retinal waves. Experimental evidence suggests that retinal waves strongly influence the emergence of sensory representations before visual experience. We aim to model this early stage of functional development by using movies of neurally active developing retinas as pre-training data for neural networks. Specifically, we pre-train a ResNet-18 with an unsupervised contrastive learning objective (SimCLR) on both simulated and experimentally-obtained movies of retinal waves, then evaluate its performance on image classification tasks. We find that pre-training on retinal waves significantly improves performance on tasks that test object invariance to spatial translation, while slightly improving performance on more complex tasks like image classification. Notably, these performance boosts are realized on held-out natural images even though the pre-training procedure does not include any natural image data. We then propose a geometrical explanation for the increase in network performance, namely that the spatiotemporal characteristics of retinal waves facilitate the formation of separable feature representations. In particular, we demonstrate that networks pre-trained on retinal waves are more effective at separating image manifolds than randomly initialized networks, especially for manifolds defined by sets of spatial translations. These findings indicate that the broad spatiotemporal properties of retinal waves prepare networks for higher order feature extraction.

papers.title: exBERT: A Visual Analysis Tool to Explore Learned Representations in Transformer Models
papers.research_question: How can we develop an interactive tool to explore learned representations and attentions in Transformer models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces EXBERT, an interactive visualization tool for exploring learned representations and attentions in Transformer models, enabling hypothesis formulation and replication of prior analyses.
papers.conclusion: EXBERT is a tool that provides interactive insights into Transformer models' representations and attentions, facilitating hypothesis generation and analysis.
papers.key_findings:
EXBERT can replicate prior findings on BERT's attention heads learning linguistic dependencies such as AUX and POBJ.
BERT's embeddings encode linguistic information progressively across layers, with verbs becoming more prominent in later layers.
EXBERT detects gender bias in GPT-2 by showing that it predicts gendered pronouns based on stereotypical associations.
GPT-2's attention heads learn syntactic structures like AUX and DOBJ dependencies, similar to BERT.
The tool allows for interactive exploration and quick hypothesis testing of model behavior through attention visualization and corpus similarity search.
papers.limitation: EXBERT only presents statistics across a small number of neighbors for a single token at a time, which may not reveal global model behavior.
papers.abstract: Large Transformer-based language models can route and reshape complex information via their multi-headed attention mechanism. Although the attention never receives explicit supervision, it can exhibit recognizable patterns following linguistic or positional information. Analyzing the learned representations and attentions is paramount to furthering our understanding of the inner workings of these models. However, analyses have to catch up with the rapid release of new models and the growing diversity of investigation techniques. To support analysis for a wide variety of models, we introduce EXBERT, a tool to help humans conduct flexible, interactive investigations and formulate hypotheses for the model-internal reasoning process. EXBERT provides insights into the meaning of the contextual representations and attention by matching a humanspecified input to similar contexts in large annotated datasets. By aggregating the annotations of the matched contexts, EXBERT can quickly replicate findings from literature and extend them to previously not analyzed models.

papers.title: Mechanistic Independence: A Principle for Identifiable Disentangled Representations
papers.research_question: Under what conditions can disentangled representations be identified without relying on statistical assumptions, by using mechanistic independence criteria?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a unified framework for disentangled representations based on mechanistic independence, proposing several independence criteria and proving identifiability theorems for latent subspaces under nonlinear, non-invertible mixing.
papers.conclusion: Mechanistic independence provides a unifying framework that clarifies the conditions for identifiability of disentangled representations without relying on statistical assumptions.
papers.key_findings:
Local disentanglement implies global disentanglement under mild topological conditions (path-connectedness and local injectivity).
Type D independence (disjoint support) yields identifiability of latent subspaces up to block-wise invertible transforms and permutations.
Type M independence (mutual non-inclusion) yields identifiability when combined with a sparsity regularizer.
Type S independence (sparsity gap) yields identifiability even when supports overlap.
Type Hn independence (vanishing cross-derivatives) yields identifiability when the generator is separable of order n.
papers.limitation: The sparsity gap condition (Type S) is intractable to optimize in practice, and finding robust surrogate losses is an open problem.
future_direction: Identifying robust surrogate losses for the sparsity gap condition (Type S).
papers.abstract: Disentangled representations seek to recover latent factors of variation underlying observed data, yet their identifiability is still not fully understood. We introduce a unified framework in which disentanglement is achieved through mechanistic independence, which characterizes latent factors by how they act on observed variables rather than by their latent distribution. This perspective is invariant to changes of the latent density, even when such changes induce statistical dependencies among factors. Within this framework, we propose several related independence criteria -- ranging from support-based and sparsity-based to higher-order conditions -- and show that each yields identifiability of latent subspaces, even under nonlinear, non-invertible mixing. We further establish a hierarchy among these criteria and provide a graph-theoretic characterization of latent subspaces as connected components. Together, these results clarify the conditions under which disentangled representations can be identified without relying on statistical assumptions.

papers.title: Consequences of Slow Neural Dynamics for Incremental Learning
papers.research_question: How does the temporal smoothness of internal states affect the efficiency of learning when the training data are also temporally smooth? How does it affect the kinds of representations that are learned?
papers.core_contribution: Networks with linear recurrence and gating learn more efficiently from temporally correlated data and can learn internal representations that separate fast and slow sources in the environment.
papers.conclusion: Intrinsic temporal autocorrelation is not an obstacle for learning but can be an inductive bias that accelerates learning and leads to more interpretable, timescale-separated representations when learning from correlated data streams.
papers.key_findings:
Feedforward networks learn slower with temporally autocorrelated data, while networks with linear recurrence learn faster.
Adding a gating mechanism to reset memory at category transitions allows recurrent networks to benefit from autocorrelation while avoiding interference from unrelated prior information.
Networks with recurrence and multiscale gating can learn internal representations that un-mix features varying on different timescales from multi-scale autocorrelated data.
The linear-recurrence-plus-gating model generalizes better across different levels of temporal autocorrelation compared to an LSTM trained with backpropagation through time.
Intrinsic temporal autocorrelation in neural dynamics can serve as a useful inductive bias for incremental learning from correlated data.
papers.limitation:
The gating mechanism in the autoencoder experiments is somewhat artificial as it requires knowing which features change quickly or slowly.
The work uses simple architectures and synthetic datasets; future work should test on larger architectures and more realistic datasets.
future_direction: Examine the efficacy of linear recurrence and gating mechanisms in CNN architectures trained on video segmentation sequences.
Test whether results generalize to larger architectures and more realistic datasets with a broader hyperparameter search.
Extend the autoencoder architecture to a predictive architecture that predicts the next stimulus rather than reconstructing the present one.
Investigate the broader consequences of learning with recurrence for reducing the difference between human internal representations and those of feedforward nets.
papers.abstract: In the human brain, internal states are often correlated over time (due to local recurrence and other intrinsic circuit properties), punctuated by abrupt transitions. At first glance, temporal smoothness of internal states presents a problem for learning input-output mappings (e.g. category labels for images), because the internal representation of the input will contain a mixture of current input and prior inputs. However, when training with naturalistic data (e.g. movies) there is also temporal autocorrelation in the input. How does the temporal "smoothness" of internal states affect the efficiency of learning when the training data are also temporally smooth? How does it affect the kinds of representations that are learned? We found that, when trained with temporally smooth data, "slow" neural networks (equipped with linear recurrence and gating mechanisms) learned to categorize more efficiently than feedforward networks. Furthermore, networks with linear recurrence and multi-timescale gating could learn internal representations that "un-mixed" quickly-varying and slowly-varying data sources. Together, these findings demonstrate how a fundamental property of cortical dynamics (their temporal autocorrelation) can serve as an inductive bias, leading to more efficient category learning and to the representational separation of fast and slow sources in the environment.

papers.title: Space as Time Through Neuron Position Learning
papers.research_question: What happens when synaptic delays are defined as Euclidean distances between neurons and neuron positions are learned? How does this space-time coupling affect network topology, functional specialization, and efficiency?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a neuron position learning algorithm that couples space and time through delays defined as Euclidean distances, leading to self-organized modular and efficient network structures with functional specialization.
papers.conclusion: Neuron position learning provides a framework for studying space-time coupling in neural networks, leading to biologically plausible structures and offering benefits for neuromorphic hardware.
papers.key_findings:
Neuron positions in the hidden layer correlate with input connectivity patterns, enabling prediction of positions from weights.
Networks with position learning rely on local computations and form circuits associated with specific tasks.
Under distance-dependent cost regularisation, networks achieve higher modularity and more efficient wiring.
Unconstrained position learning converges on solutions with more local connections, making them robust to pruning of long delays.
Position learning reduces the number of free parameters compared to direct delay learning while maintaining performance.
papers.limitation:
The study focuses on small networks, which may not reflect scaling behavior.
Neurons can be arbitrarily close, unlike biological volume exclusion, which could be addressed by adding repulsive forces.
future_direction: Introduce repulsive forces between neurons to prevent arbitrary closeness.
Extend analysis to modular tasks with added temporal structure, multimodal settings, or multi-task problems.
Combine position learning with structural plasticity algorithms like DEEP R to yield interesting network geometries.
papers.abstract: Biological neural networks exist in physical space where distance influences communication delays: a fundamental coupling between space and time absent in most artificial neural networks. While recent work has separately explored spatial embeddings and learnable synaptic delays in spiking neural networks, we unify these approaches through a novel neuron position learning algorithm where delays relate to the Euclidean distances between neurons. We derive gradients with respect to neuron positions and demonstrate that this biologically-motivated constraint acts as an inductive bias: networks trained on temporal classification tasks spontaneously self-organize into local, clustered topologies and a modular, efficiently wired structure emerges if connection costs are distance-dependent. Remarkably, we observe functional specialization aligned with spatial clustering without explicitly enforcing it. These findings lay the groundwork for networks in which space and time are intrinsically coupled, offering new avenues for mechanistic interpretability, biologically inspired modelling, and efficient implementations.

papers.title: SOM-VAE: Interpretable Discrete Representation Learning on Time Series
papers.research_question: How to learn interpretable discrete representations of time series that are smooth and provide superior clustering performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces SOM-VAE, a framework for learning interpretable discrete representations of time series, featuring a gradient-based self-organizing map and an integrated Markov model for temporal smoothness and improved clustering.
papers.conclusion: SOM-VAE can recover topologically interpretable state representations on time series and static data, improves clustering performance over standard methods, and offers interpretable visualizations that could aid in domains like healthcare.
papers.key_findings:
SOM-VAE outperforms baselines like k-means, VQ-VAE, and traditional SOM in clustering performance on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST in terms of purity and NMI.
The gradient-based SOM training (GB-SOM) performs better than the original SOM algorithm.
The probabilistic Markov model can be learned concurrently with the SOM-VAE and improves clustering performance on noisy data, such as medical time series.
On the chaotic Lorenz system, SOM-VAE learns interpretable representations that capture the macro-states (attractor basins) while ignoring chaotic noise.
On real medical data from the eICU database, SOM-VAE-prob learns representations that are informative for downstream prediction tasks and provides interpretable visualizations of patient trajectories.
future_direction: Extend the probabilistic component for predictions using higher-order Markov Models, Hidden Markov Models, or Gaussian Processes.
Find more theoretically principled ways to overcome the non-differentiability in discrete representation learning.
Learn the neighborhood structure as a graph directly from data instead of fixing a latent space structure like a 2D grid.
papers.abstract: High-dimensional time series are common in many domains. Since human cognition is not optimized to work well in high-dimensional spaces, these areas could benefit from interpretable low-dimensional representations. However, most representation learning algorithms for time series data are difficult to interpret. This is due to non-intuitive mappings from data features to salient properties of the representation and non-smoothness over time. To address this problem, we propose a new representation learning framework building on ideas from interpretable discrete dimensionality reduction and deep generative modeling. This framework allows us to learn discrete representations of time series, which give rise to smooth and interpretable embeddings with superior clustering performance. We introduce a new way to overcome the non-differentiability in discrete representation learning and present a gradient-based version of the traditional self-organizing map algorithm that is more performant than the original. Furthermore, to allow for a probabilistic interpretation of our method, we integrate a Markov model in the representation space. This model uncovers the temporal transition structure, improves clustering performance even further and provides additional explanatory insights as well as a natural representation of uncertainty. We evaluate our model in terms of clustering performance and interpretability on static (Fashion-)MNIST data, a time series of linearly interpolated (Fashion-)MNIST images, a chaotic Lorenz attractor system with two macro states, as well as on a challenging real world medical time series application on the eICU data set. Our learned representations compare favorably with competitor methods and facilitate downstream tasks on the real world data.

papers.title: Towards scientific discovery with dictionary learning: Extracting biological concepts from microscopy foundation models
papers.research_question: Can dictionary learning extract meaningful high-level concepts from unsupervised vision foundation models trained on scientific data (cell microscopy images) where prior knowledge about concepts is limited?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ICFL, a novel sparse dictionary learning algorithm combined with PCA whitening, to successfully extract biologically meaningful concepts (e.g., cell types, genetic perturbations) from frozen representations of vision foundation models trained on cell microscopy images.
papers.conclusion: Dictionary learning, specifically ICFL with PCA whitening, is a powerful and promising approach for extracting interpretable biological concepts from microscopy foundation models, enabling new directions for scientific discovery via mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
ICFL combined with PCA whitening extracts sparse features that correlate with biological concepts such as cell types and genetic perturbations.
ICFL reduces the number of 'dead features' compared to TopK SAEs.
Linear probes on reconstructions from ICFL features preserve significant biological information, with accuracies comparable to probes on original representations.
ICFL features achieve selectivity scores comparable to handcrafted CellProfiler features for identifying genetic perturbations.
Token-level heatmaps from feature directions enable interpretation of subtle morphological changes, such as distinguishing perturbed from control-like cells.
future_direction: Assess whether peak selectivity of handcrafted features can be matched using deep learning-based approaches with fewer non-zero elements.
Future research on interpreting and validating concept directions found in large foundation models for microscopy image data.
papers.abstract: Sparse dictionary learning (DL) has emerged as a powerful approach to extract semantically meaningful concepts from the internals of large language models (LLMs) trained mainly in the text domain. In this work, we explore whether DL can extract meaningful concepts from less human-interpretable scientific data, such as vision foundation models trained on cell microscopy images, where limited prior knowledge exists about which high-level concepts should arise. We propose a novel combination of a sparse DL algorithm, Iterative Codebook Feature Learning (ICFL), with a PCA whitening pre-processing step derived from control data. Using this combined approach, we successfully retrieve biologically meaningful concepts, such as cell types and genetic perturbations. Moreover, we demonstrate how our method reveals subtle morphological changes arising from human-interpretable interventions, offering a promising new direction for scientific discovery via mechanistic interpretability in bioimaging.

papers.title: Transformers learn factored representations
papers.research_question: Do transformers learn to factor their world into parts from next-token prediction, and why would they have an inductive bias for factored representations?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers learn to factor their world into parts, representing each factor in orthogonal subspaces of the residual stream, and show an inductive bias toward factored representations even when it is lossy.
papers.conclusion: Transformers decompose the world into parts and represent them in orthogonal subspaces due to an inductive bias from next-token prediction, suggesting interpretable low-dimensional structure may persist in models trained on complex data.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers learn factored representations in orthogonal subspaces when data has conditionally independent factors.
The dimensionality of activations collapses to the linearly growing factored prediction, not the exponentially growing joint representation.
Factor subspaces become approximately orthogonal over training, as measured by subspace overlap and dimensionality additivity.
Factoring begins at the token embedding layer, with the embedding matrix developing low-rank structure corresponding to factor subspaces.
Transformers exhibit an inductive bias toward factored representations, learning them early even when data is not perfectly factorable, sacrificing fidelity for dimensional efficiency.
papers.limitation: Experiments are conducted on synthetic data with known latent structure, which may not fully capture real-world complexity.
future_direction: Investigate whether differences in factorization behavior between transformers, RNNs, and LSTMs are due to training dynamics or inductive bias.
papers.abstract: Transformers pretrained via next token prediction learn to factor their world into parts, representing these factors in orthogonal subspaces of the residual stream. We formalize two representational hypotheses: (1) a representation in the product space of all factors, whose dimension grows exponentially with the number of parts, or (2) a factored representation in orthogonal subspaces, whose dimension grows linearly. The factored representation is lossless when factors are conditionally independent, but sacrifices predictive fidelity otherwise, creating a tradeoff between dimensional efficiency and accuracy. We derive precise predictions about the geometric structure of activations for each, including the number of subspaces, their dimensionality, and the arrangement of context embeddings within them. We test between these hypotheses on transformers trained on synthetic processes with known latent structure. Models learn factored representations when factors are conditionally independent, and continue to favor them early in training even when noise or hidden dependencies undermine conditional independence, reflecting an inductive bias toward factoring at the cost of fidelity. This provides a principled explanation for why transformers decompose the world into parts, and suggests that interpretable low dimensional structure may persist even in models trained on complex data.

papers.title: What Does BERT Learn about the Structure of Language?
papers.research_question: What linguistic structure does BERT learn? Specifically, can we unveil the representations learned by BERT to proto-linguistics structures?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides evidence that BERT captures hierarchical linguistic structure, with surface features in lower layers, syntactic in middle, and semantic in higher layers, and that it uses deeper layers for long-distance dependencies and implicitly captures tree-like structures.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that BERT captures structural properties of English language, with a hierarchy of linguistic signals and compositional modeling that parallels traditional syntactic analysis.
papers.key_findings:
BERT's phrasal representation captures phrase-level information in the lower layers, which gets diluted in higher layers.
BERT embeds a rich hierarchy of linguistic signals: surface information at the bottom, syntactic in the middle, and semantic at the top.
BERT requires deeper layers to handle long-distance dependency information, such as subject-verb agreement with more attractors.
BERT implicitly implements a tree-based compositional scheme, as shown by Tensor Product Decomposition Networks (TPDN) approximating BERT's representations.
The untrained version of BERT in higher layers outperforms the trained version in predicting sentence length, indicating that training trades off basic surface features for more complex information.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to English and may not generalize to other languages or noisy user-generated content.
future_direction: Investigating if the results transfer to other domains with higher syntactic variability, such as noisy user-generated content or morphologically-rich languages.
papers.abstract: BERT is a recent language representation model that has surprisingly performed well in diverse language understanding benchmarks. This result indicates the possibility that BERT networks capture structural information about language. In this work, we provide novel support for this claim by performing a series of experiments to unpack the elements of English language structure learned by BERT. We first show that BERT's phrasal representation captures phrase-level information in the lower layers. We also show that BERT's intermediate layers encode a rich hierarchy of linguistic information, with surface features at the bottom, syntactic features in the middle and semantic features at the top. BERT turns out to require deeper layers when long-distance dependency information is required, e.g. to track subjectverb agreement. Finally, we show that BERT representations capture linguistic information in a compositional way that mimics classical, tree-like structures.

papers.title: Insights on representational similarity in neural networks with\n canonical correlation
papers.research_question: How can we compare neural network representations and how do they evolve over time?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces projection weighted CCA, an improved method for comparing neural network representations, and uses it to show that generalizing networks converge to more similar representations than memorizing networks, wider networks converge to more similar solutions, and RNNs exhibit bottom-up convergence during training.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates the utility of projection weighted CCA for analyzing neural network representations, revealing insights about convergence and similarity in CNNs and RNNs.
papers.key_findings:
Networks that generalize converge to more similar representations than those that memorize.
Wider networks converge to more similar solutions than narrower networks.
Networks with identical topology but different learning rates converge to distinct clusters of solutions.
RNNs exhibit bottom-up convergence over the course of training.
RNN hidden states vary nonlinearly across sequence timesteps.
future_direction: Examine what is unique about directions preserved across networks trained with different initializations.
Explore whether the insight that similar solutions lead to higher generalization could be used as a regularizer.
Investigate which aspects of RNN representations are stable over time and which vary.
papers.abstract:
Comparing different neural network representations and determining how
representations evolve over time remain challenging open questions in our
understanding of the function of neural networks. Comparing representations in
neural networks is fundamentally difficult as the structure of representations
varies greatly, even across groups of networks trained on identical tasks, and
over the course of training. Here, we develop projection weighted CCA
(Canonical Correlation Analysis) as a tool for understanding neural networks,
building off of SVCCA, a recently proposed method (Raghu et al., 2017). We
first improve the core method, showing how to differentiate between signal and
noise, and then apply this technique to compare across a group of CNNs,
demonstrating that networks which generalize converge to more similar
representations than networks which memorize, that wider networks converge to
more similar solutions than narrow networks, and that trained networks with
identical topology but different learning rates converge to distinct clusters
with diverse representations. We also investigate the representational dynamics
of RNNs, across both training and sequential timesteps, finding that RNNs
converge in a bottom-up pattern over the course of training and that the hidden
state is highly variable over the course of a sequence, even when accounting
for linear transforms. Together, these results provide new insights into the
function of CNNs and RNNs, and demonstrate the utility of using CCA to
understand representations.

papers.title: Uncovering Emergent Physics Representations Learned In-Context by Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do large language models implicitly learn physics during in-context learning, and do recognizable physical quantities emerge as distinct features in their internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that large language models can learn to forecast physical dynamics via in-context learning, and that energy-related features emerge in their residual stream activations, which are causally important for accurate predictions.
papers.conclusion: The results demonstrate that LLMs can internalize physical concepts like energy during in-context learning, suggesting transformer architectures can internalize abstract reasoning priors similar to human abstraction.
papers.key_findings:
Prediction accuracy for physical dynamics forecasting improves with longer context length.
Sparse activations from sparse autoencoders (SAEs) applied to residual streams correlate with energy quantities (total, kinetic, potential).
The correlation between sparse activations and energy is context-dependent and increases with longer contexts, especially for chaotic systems.
Intervention experiments ablating energy-correlated sparse activations degrade prediction accuracy, indicating their functional role.
Energy-related features are most prominently captured in the middle layers of the transformer.
papers.limitation: The study uses raw trajectory values as the sole input modality without external instructions or prompting strategies, leaving open whether chain-of-thought or structured prompts would strengthen correlations.
future_direction: Explore physics concepts beyond classical mechanics.
Investigate more human-aligned tasks such as answering conceptual questions from physics exams.
Leverage physics-informed tasks to understand internal mechanisms of large-scale models and advance LLM-based agents for physically realistic environments.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit impressive in-context learning (ICL) abilities, enabling them to solve wide range of tasks via textual prompts alone. As these capabilities advance, the range of applicable domains continues to expand significantly. However, identifying the precise mechanisms or internal structures within LLMs that allow successful ICL across diverse, distinct classes of tasks remains elusive. Physics-based tasks offer a promising testbed for probing this challenge. Unlike synthetic sequences such as basic arithmetic or symbolic equations, physical systems provide experimentally controllable, real-world data based on structured dynamics grounded in fundamental principles. This makes them particularly suitable for studying the emergent reasoning behaviors of LLMs in a realistic yet tractable setting. Here, we mechanistically investigate the ICL ability of LLMs, especially focusing on their ability to reason about physics. Using a dynamics forecasting task in physical systems as a proxy, we evaluate whether LLMs can learn physics in context. We first show that the performance of dynamics forecasting in context improves with longer input contexts. To uncover how such capability emerges in LLMs, we analyze the model's residual stream activations using sparse autoencoders (SAEs). Our experiments reveal that the features captured by SAEs correlate with key physical variables, such as energy. These findings demonstrate that meaningful physical concepts are encoded within LLMs during in-context learning. In sum, our work provides a novel case study that broadens our understanding of how LLMs learn in context.

papers.title: Causal-oriented representation learning for time-series forecasting based on the spatiotemporal information transformation
papers.research_question: How can causal analysis and multistep forecasting be jointly performed from a unified perspective to understand system dynamics?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Causal-oriented Representation Learning Predictor (CReP), a neural network framework that jointly conducts causal analysis and multistep forecasting from a unified perspective.
papers.conclusion: CReP effectively achieves multi-step-ahead forecasting and infers causal networks for target variables, offering a comprehensive understanding of system dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
CReP demonstrates satisfactory forecasting performance with low RMSE and high PCC on simulation models like Lorenz 96.
The framework successfully infers cause and effect networks for target variables, aligning with known causal structures.
CReP applies to real-world datasets, such as cardiovascular inpatients and COVID-19 spread, providing practical insights.
Ablation studies show that all loss components (reconstruction, future-consistency, orthogonal) are necessary for optimal performance.
The method is self-supervised and handles nonlinearity and non-separability better than Granger causality-based approaches.
papers.abstract: In real-world high-dimensional systems, both causal dependencies and temporal information of key variables are essential for dissecting the underlying mechanisms governing system dynamics. However, effective approaches to synthesize these two interconnected aspects for deeper insights remain lacking. Here we show a neural network framework, the Causal-oriented Representation Learning Predictor (CReP), which jointly conducts causal analysis and multistep forecasting from a unified perspective. CReP implicitly learns latent causal representations from observed data while simultaneously making multistep predictions, and explicitly interprets the representations to uncover the causes and effects of target variable. The core idea of CReP is to decompose the original space into three orthogonal latent factors, each capturing distinct causal representations: cause-related, effect-related, and non-causal representations of the target variable. The reconstruction-based dynamic causation, generalized through spatiotemporal information (STI) transformation mechanism, provides a theoretical foundation for simultaneously modeling causal interactions via latent representations and predicting future states using the effect representation. Evaluations on three simulation models and two real-world datasets demonstrate CReP’s robust forecasting accuracy and reliable causal insights. As a self-supervised-learning approach, CReP shows significant potential for practical applications and provides a unified framework to reveal intrinsic mechanisms in dynamical systems by integrating causal relationships and temporal information. In complex high-dimensional systems like power grids or COVID-19 transmission, both causal dependencies and temporal information of key variables are essential for dissecting the underlying mechanisms governing system dynamics. This paper presents Causal-oriented Representation Learning Predictor, a neural network framework designed to jointly conduct causal analysis and multistep forecasting.

papers.title: Decomposing Representation Space into Interpretable Subspaces with Unsupervised Learning
papers.research_question: Can we find interpretable subspaces in neural representations in an unsupervised way? To what extent are different aspects organized in separate subspaces?
